section.title: Judaism: Beliefs
section.blurb: Jewish beliefs and teachings about God, the afterlife, the Messiah, the covenants, moral principles, sanctity of life, and free will and the mitzvot.

spec.point: Judaism is one of the diverse religious traditions in Great Britain; the main religious tradition in Great Britain is Christianity

topics.title: The nature of God: God as One and creator
topics.overview: Belief in one God who created everything is the foundation of Judaism, and it shapes how Jews worship, pray and see the purpose of life.

bullets: Jews are **monotheists**: they believe in one God only, who is eternal, all-powerful and has no body or physical form.
God is **indivisible**: not made of parts, so Jews reject the Christian idea of the Trinity.
The **Shema** (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the Jewish declaration of faith, said morning and evening. It begins 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One'.
The first commandment forbids worshipping any other god or idol (Exodus 20:3).
Maimonides' 13 Principles of Faith start with belief that God exists, is the creator and is One.
Genesis 1 says God created the heavens and earth in six days and rested on the seventh (Shabbat). God said creation was 'very good'.
Most Jews believe God created from nothing (**ex nihilo**), which shows God's unlimited power.
Jews believe God did not just create once: God also **sustains** creation every day (Isaiah 45:7).
Humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), so every person has value and purpose.
Humans are given **stewardship**: a duty to look after God's world (Psalm 24:1, 'The earth is the Lord's').
Many Orthodox Jews read Genesis 1 as a true account of how God created.
Many Reform Jews accept science (such as the Big Bang and evolution) and see Genesis as teaching that God is behind creation and that it has purpose, not as a science textbook.
God is **eternal** (no beginning or end), **omnipotent** (all-powerful) and **omniscient** (all-knowing).
God is **transcendent** (beyond the universe and greater than it) but also **immanent** (close and involved in the world).
Because God has no body, Judaism forbids any picture or statue of God. Synagogues have no images of God.
Out of respect, many Jews avoid saying or writing God's name in full, and say 'Hashem' ('the Name') or write 'G-d'.

The Shema goes on: 'Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might' (Deuteronomy 6:5). Its words are placed in the **mezuzah** on doorposts and in **tefillin**.

notes.h: How these beliefs influence Jews today
bullets: Saying the Shema morning and night, and teaching it to children (Deuteronomy 6:7). It is traditionally the last words a Jew says before death.
Saying **berakhot** (blessings) that praise God as 'King of the universe' before eating, or when seeing a rainbow or the sea.
Keeping **Shabbat** as a weekly reminder that God created the world and rested on the seventh day.
Celebrating **Rosh Hashanah**, which the rabbis link to the creation of the world (the 'birthday of the world').
Caring for the environment and animals, because 'the earth is the Lord's' (Psalm 24:1). Some Jews plant trees at **Tu B'Shevat**, the new year for trees.
Treating every human as valuable, because all are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27).
Christianity is the main religious tradition in Great Britain. Christians also believe in one God but describe God as a Trinity (Father, Son and Holy Spirit).
Jews reject the Trinity and the idea that God became human, because God is One, indivisible and has no body.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Many take Genesis literally or as a divinely revealed account. Belief in God as One and Creator is a fixed, non-negotiable principle of faith.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Accept scientific explanations of how the universe developed, while still believing God is the creator who gave it meaning and purpose. Genesis is read as teaching, not science.

topics.title: The nature of God: Law-Giver, Judge, loving and merciful
topics.overview: Jews believe God gave the Law, judges how people live, and is both just and merciful. This explains why Jews keep the mitzvot and take repentance seriously.

bullets: God gave laws from the beginning: to Adam, to Noah (7 Noahide laws) and most importantly to Moses at Mount Sinai.
The **Torah** contains the **613 mitzvot** (commandments), including the Ten Commandments.
Jews believe the laws are for their good (Deuteronomy 10:12-13) and show how to live a holy life.
Keeping the mitzvot is a way of keeping the covenant with God.
God is a just judge who knows everything a person has done (Genesis 18:25, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?').
Jews believe God judges people on **Rosh Hashanah** (New Year) and **Yom Kippur**, and also after death.
God judges by how well people followed the mitzvot and treated others.
God is not only strict: Exodus 34:6 describes God as 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, rich in kindness'.
God forgives those who sincerely repent (**teshuvah**, meaning 'returning' to God).
Justice and mercy work together: Jews believe God judges fairly but wants people to change, not to be punished.

notes.h: Judgement during the year: the Days of Awe
bullets: Jewish tradition teaches that on **Rosh Hashanah** God opens the books of judgement and writes each person's fate for the coming year.
The ten **Days of Awe** that follow are a chance for teshuvah (repentance), prayer and tzedakah (charity).
On **Yom Kippur** (the Day of Atonement) the judgement is sealed. Jews fast, confess and ask forgiveness.
Jews greet each other with the wish to be 'written and sealed for a good year'.
God forgives sins against God, but for sins against people a Jew must first put things right with the person they hurt.

notes.h: How these beliefs influence Jews today
bullets: Jews keep the mitzvot because they come from God, the Law-Giver, and they study Torah to know what God requires.
Belief in a fair Judge gives Jews confidence that wrongs will be put right, even if not in this life.
Belief in God's mercy encourages Jews to repent rather than despair, and to forgive others as God forgives them.
Jewish courts (Beth Din) and Jewish ethics stress fair judgement, because humans should copy God's justice and mercy.
Many Jews pray 'Avinu Malkeinu' ('Our Father, our King') during the Days of Awe, showing God as both loving parent and judge.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: The 613 mitzvot are God's binding commands, given at Sinai, and must be followed as written. God's judgement is based on obedience to the Law.

views.label: Reform
views.text: The mitzvot are important guidance, but each Jew uses informed free will to decide which to follow. God's role as loving and merciful is often stressed alongside judgement.

Avoid Christian ideas such as Jesus judging the world. In Judaism God alone is the Judge.

topics.title: The divine presence: the Shekhinah
topics.overview: The Shekhinah is the idea that although God cannot be seen, God's presence can be felt among people. It gives Jews comfort and a sense that God is close.

bullets: **Shekhinah** means 'the dwelling' or 'divine presence': God's presence felt in the world.
The word is not in the Tenakh itself but is used by the rabbis in the Talmud and Midrash.
In Hebrew it is a feminine word, so the Shekhinah is often described in a motherly way: caring, comforting and sharing in suffering.
The burning bush that spoke to Moses (Exodus 3).
The pillar of cloud by day and pillar of fire by night that guided the Israelites out of Egypt (Exodus 13:21).
God's presence on Mount Sinai.
God's glory filling the Tabernacle and then Solomon's Temple.
Ezekiel 43:2 says 'the earth shone with His glory'.
The rabbis taught the Shekhinah went into exile with the Jews, so God never abandons them.
Jews believe the Shekhinah is present when ten people (a **minyan**) pray or when people study Torah together (Pirkei Avot 3:6).
It gives comfort in hard times, for example in the Holocaust or in personal suffering.

notes.h: The Tabernacle, the Temple and the Western Wall
bullets: When the Tabernacle was finished, a cloud covered it and 'the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle' (Exodus 40:34).
The same happened when King Solomon's Temple was dedicated in Jerusalem (1 Kings 8:10-11). The Holy of Holies was seen as the place where God's presence dwelt.

After the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE, a Jewish tradition taught that the Shekhinah never left the **Western Wall**, the last remaining part of the Temple compound. Many Jews pray there and leave written prayers in the cracks.
The **ner tamid** (ever-burning light) above the ark in a synagogue recalls the light in the Temple and is often linked to God's constant presence.
The Talmud (Berakhot 6a) teaches that when ten people pray together the divine presence is with them, which supports the importance of a **minyan**.
Pirkei Avot 3:6 goes further: the Shekhinah is present even when one person studies Torah.
Some Jews, especially in the mystical (Kabbalah) tradition, describe the Shekhinah as the feminine side of God that shares the suffering of the Jewish people in exile.
The Shekhinah is not a second god or a separate being: Jews stress it is the presence of the one God. AQA papers sometimes spell it **Shekinah**.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Stress that the Shekhinah is specially present in synagogue prayer with a minyan and in Torah study, and look forward to it fully returning when the Temple is rebuilt.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Tend to see the Shekhinah as a symbol of God's closeness to everyone, felt in worship, nature, community and moral action, rather than in a rebuilt Temple.

Do not call the ner tamid a candle that 'is' God. It is a light that symbolises God's constant presence.

topics.title: Life after death, judgement and resurrection
topics.overview: Jewish teaching about the afterlife is varied and not fixed, so Jews tend to focus on living well now. Know the main views and the Orthodox and Reform differences.

bullets: Judaism teaches that this life (**Olam Ha-Zeh**) matters most. The Tenakh says little about what happens after death.
**Olam Ha-Ba** ('the world to come') is the afterlife or future age where the righteous are with God.

**Sheol** (in the Tenakh) is a dark, shadowy place of the dead. **Gan Eden** is paradise. **Gehinnom** is a place where souls are cleansed, traditionally for up to 12 months, not usually eternal punishment.
Many Jews believe each person is judged by God for how they kept the mitzvot and treated others, some at death and some on a final Day of Judgement.
The soul is believed to come from God, so it is eternal.
Maimonides' 13th principle says God will bring the dead back to life.
Many Orthodox Jews believe in **bodily resurrection** at the end of time, which is why they bury the dead and do not cremate.
Many Reform Jews believe in the **immortality of the soul**, not a physical resurrection, so some accept cremation.
Some Jews (especially Kabbalists and Hasidic Jews) believe in **gilgul**: souls are reborn to complete unfinished mitzvot and help heal the world.
Belief in judgement encourages Jews to keep the mitzvot and do good deeds.
Because the afterlife is uncertain, Jews put effort into **Tikkun Olam** (healing the world) now.
Belief in resurrection or the eternal soul shapes funeral practice and gives comfort to the bereaved.

The Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16b) describes three groups: the wholly righteous, the wholly wicked and the 'in-between', which is most people. This idea is used both for yearly judgement and for judgement after death.
Some Jews believe judgement happens straight after death; others believe in a final Day of Judgement after the Messiah comes and the dead are raised.

The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 10:1) teaches that 'all Israel have a share in the world to come', and Maimonides taught that the righteous of all nations also have a share. So a good life, not being Jewish, is what matters.
A soul may spend time in Gehinnom being cleansed before entering Gan Eden. Only the very wicked are believed by some to be destroyed or to stay in remorse.
The Reform Pittsburgh Platform (1885) affirmed that 'the soul is immortal' but rejected bodily resurrection and Gehenna and Eden as places of eternal punishment and reward.
Some Reform and Liberal prayer books changed the Amidah blessing praising God 'who revives the dead' to wording such as 'who gives life to all'.
Many Reform and Liberal Jews say what happens after death is in God's hands, and stress how life is lived now.
Orthodox Jews bury the body quickly and whole, and do not cremate, out of respect for the body God created and in hope of resurrection.

Mourners say the **Kaddish** prayer for a parent for 11 months, partly in the belief that it helps the soul. It is not said for 12 months, since that would suggest the parent needed the longest cleansing.
Belief that 'only Torah and good deeds' go with a person (Pirkei Avot 6:9) encourages Jews to live well now.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Affirm bodily resurrection when the Messiah comes, and judgement of every soul. Burial is required.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Stress the soul's immortality and judgement, but reject a physical resurrection. Many leave the details open and focus on life now.

views.label: Kabbalist and Hasidic
views.text: A soul may return to earth in a new body (gilgul) to complete mitzvot it did not fulfil and to help repair the world, as an act of God's compassion.

Gilgul is not Hindu reincarnation: it is the soul returning to complete mitzvot and help heal the world. And do not write about funeral customs unless you link them to a belief about life after death.

topics.title: The nature and role of the Messiah
topics.overview: The Messiah is a future leader who will bring peace and justice. Jews hold different views on whether this is a person or a time, and this shapes how they act now.

bullets: **Mashiach** means 'anointed one': kings were anointed with oil.
Traditional belief: a human leader, descended from **King David**, sent by God (Jeremiah 23:5).
He will gather Jews back to Israel, rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, bring justice and bring the world to know God.
Belief that the Messiah will come is one of Maimonides' 13 Principles of Faith.
Jews pray for the Messiah in the daily Amidah prayer.
A future time of world peace: 'nation will not lift up sword against nation' (Isaiah 2:4).
No war, hunger or hatred, and everyone will worship the One God.
Some Jews believe the dead will be resurrected at this time.
Most **Orthodox** Jews expect a literal, personal Messiah and a rebuilt Temple.
**Reform** Jews usually do not expect a personal Messiah. They believe the Messianic Age will come through humans working together for justice and peace.
Jews do not believe Jesus was the Messiah, because the Messianic Age of peace has not happened.
Hope that things will improve helps Jews through persecution and hardship.
Orthodox Jews keep the mitzvot closely, believing this brings the Messiah closer.
Reform Jews are influenced to work for justice, peace and **Tikkun Olam** to help bring the Messianic Age.
In Judaism the Messiah is a **human** being, not God and not divine.
The Messiah is not a saviour who dies for people's sins. Jews believe each person returns to God through teshuvah (repentance).
The Messiah does not judge the dead: **God alone** is the Judge.
Jews do not accept Jesus as the Messiah because the Messianic tasks (world peace, rebuilding the Temple, gathering the exiles) have not been fulfilled.
A **king** from the line of David who rules with wisdom and justice (Jeremiah 23:5, Isaiah 11:1-5).
A great **teacher of Torah** who leads all Jews to keep the mitzvot.
**Gathering the exiles**: bringing Jews from around the world back to the land of Israel (Ezekiel 36:24).
**Rebuilding the Temple** in Jerusalem.
Bringing **world peace**, when 'nation shall not take up sword against nation' (Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:3), and a world where 'the wolf shall dwell with the lamb' (Isaiah 11:6).
Bringing all people to recognise the one God (Zechariah 14:9).
Some Orthodox Jews teach that in every generation there is someone who could be the Messiah, if the world is worthy.
The Reform Pittsburgh Platform (1885) spoke of a 'Messianic hope' for an age of truth, justice and peace for all, rather than a personal king.
Some Reform prayer books changed the Amidah's request for a 'redeemer' to a prayer for 'redemption', showing hope for a Messianic Age rather than a person.
Some religious Zionist Jews see the modern State of Israel as a first step towards redemption, while a small number of strictly Orthodox Jews believe a Jewish state should wait for the Messiah.
Most Jews of all traditions agree that people should work and pray for a better world now.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: A personal Messiah from David's line will come, rebuild the Temple and gather the exiles. Keeping the mitzvot and praying prepare the world for this.

views.label: Reform
views.text: No personal Messiah. The Messianic Age is a hope for a better world that humans must work to create through justice, peace and care for creation.

views.label: Religious Zionist
views.text: The founding of the modern State of Israel and the return of Jews to the land are seen as the first steps towards redemption.

topics.title: The Promised Land and the Covenant with Abraham
topics.overview: God's covenant with Abraham created the Jewish people and promised them land. It explains why Jews see themselves as chosen, why circumcision matters and why Israel is special.

bullets: A **covenant** is a binding agreement between God and people, with promises and duties on both sides.
Abram lived in Ur and then Haran. God told him: 'Go from your country... to the land I will show you' (Genesis 12:1). Abram trusted God and went to Canaan, a model of faith for Jews.

**Genesis 12:1-3** (the passage AQA names) contains God's promises: to make Abram a **great nation**, to **bless** him and make his name great, that he would **be a blessing**, that God would bless those who bless him and curse those who curse him, and that 'all the families of the earth' would be blessed through him.
In Genesis 15 God promised descendants as many as the stars (15:5) and warned they would be strangers and slaves in another land for 400 years before being freed.
In Genesis 17 God confirmed the covenant: Abram became **Abraham** ('father of many nations') and Sarai became **Sarah**. God promised the land of Canaan 'as an everlasting possession' (17:8).
Abraham's side: worship only the one God, 'walk before me and be blameless' (17:1) and circumcise every male as the **sign of the covenant** (17:10-11).
God kept the promise of a son: Sarah gave birth to **Isaac** in old age, and the covenant passed to Isaac and then to Jacob (Israel).

notes.h: Not part of the covenant: the binding of Isaac
bullets: Genesis 22 tells how God tested Abraham by asking him to sacrifice Isaac and then provided a ram. It shows Abraham's faith and obedience.
AQA mark schemes do NOT credit the binding of Isaac as part of the covenant itself, so only use it as extra background about Abraham's faith.
The land of Canaan is now the land of **Israel**. Jerusalem is the holiest city in Judaism.
For centuries Jews have prayed facing Jerusalem, and the Passover Seder ends with 'Next year in Jerusalem'.
Moving to Israel is called **aliyah** ('going up'). The State of Israel was founded in 1948, and its Law of Return (1950) gives Jews the right to settle there.

Some Jews see living in the land as a mitzvah. Others believe Jews can live a full Jewish life anywhere, including Britain. Jews hold a wide range of views about the modern State of Israel and its politics.
Jews see themselves as the **chosen people**: chosen for responsibility, to keep the mitzvot and be 'a light to the nations' (Isaiah 42:6), not because they are better than others.
**Brit Milah** (circumcision on the eighth day) continues the covenant in every generation of Jewish boys.
The covenant gives Jews a shared identity, history and purpose. Abraham is called 'Avraham Avinu' (Abraham our father).
Abraham's trust in God encourages Jews to keep faith in hard times.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: The covenant is eternal and binding. The land of Israel was given to the Jews by God, and the mitzvot must be kept as part of the covenant.

views.label: Reform
views.text: The covenant is a close relationship that calls Jews to moral action. Many see being 'chosen' as a duty to serve humanity, and views on the land and Israel vary.

topics.title: The covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments
topics.overview: At Mount Sinai God gave Moses the Torah, including the Ten Commandments. This is the heart of Jewish law and identity.

notes.h: Moses and the covenant at Sinai
bullets: Moses was raised in Egypt, was chosen by God at the burning bush and led the Israelites out of slavery.
Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites reached **Mount Sinai**, where God made a covenant with them (Exodus 19).
The people agreed: 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exodus 24:7).
God's promise: the Jews will be His 'treasured possession' and a 'holy nation'. The people's promise: keep the mitzvot.
The sign of the Mosaic covenant is **Shabbat** (Exodus 31:16-17).
Moses is the greatest prophet and teacher. Many Orthodox Jews believe he received both the Written Torah and the Oral Torah at Sinai.
Judaism counts 'I am the Lord your God who brought you out of Egypt' as the first commandment.
Mitzvot between **people and God**: one God, no idols, do not misuse God's name, keep Shabbat.
Mitzvot between **people and people**: honour parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie about others or be jealous of what others have.
They are part of the 613 mitzvot and are read in the synagogue and displayed above the ark.
The covenant gives Jews their identity as a people with a mission.
Jews keep Shabbat, respect parents and treat others fairly because God commanded it at Sinai.
The covenant is seen as lasting for ever, so each generation takes it on (for example at Bar and Bat Mitzvah).
Born to Israelite slaves in Egypt, hidden in a basket on the Nile and raised in Pharaoh's palace.
After fleeing to Midian, God called him at the **burning bush** (Exodus 3) to free the Israelites.
He spoke for God before Pharaoh, announced the ten plagues and led the people out of Egypt (the **Exodus**) and through the Sea of Reeds (Red Sea).

On Mount Sinai he received the Torah and the two tablets of the Ten Commandments. After the people worshipped the golden calf he broke the tablets, prayed for the people's forgiveness and received a second set.
He led the Israelites for 40 years in the wilderness but died before entering the Promised Land.

'Never again did there arise in Israel a prophet like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face' (Deuteronomy 34:10). Maimonides' 7th principle says Moses is the greatest of the prophets. Jews call him **Moshe Rabbenu** ('Moses our teacher').

notes.h: The Ten Commandments in Jewish numbering (Exodus 20:1-17)
bullets: 1. I am the Lord your God who brought you out of Egypt. 2. No other gods and no idols. 3. Do not misuse God's name. 4. Remember Shabbat and keep it holy. 5. Honour your father and mother.
6. Do not murder. 7. Do not commit adultery. 8. Do not steal. 9. Do not give false evidence against your neighbour. 10. Do not covet (be jealous of) what belongs to others.
Traditionally the first tablet held commandments 1 to 5 (about God, with honouring parents seen as linked to honouring God) and the second tablet 6 to 10 (about other people).
Christians number the commandments differently, so be careful to use the Jewish order in a Judaism answer.
Many Orthodox Jews believe the whole Torah was given word for word by God to Moses (**Torah from heaven**), along with the Oral Torah later written in the Mishnah and Talmud.
Many Reform Jews believe the Torah was inspired by God but written by humans over time, so its laws can be reinterpreted (**progressive revelation**).
The festival of **Shavuot** celebrates the giving of the Torah at Sinai; the Ten Commandments are read in synagogue and some stay up all night studying Torah.
Each Bar or Bat Mitzvah is seen as a young Jew personally taking on the covenant made at Sinai.

views.label: Reform

topics.title: Key moral principles in Judaism
topics.overview: Justice, healing the world, charity and kindness guide how Jews treat others and the world. They link belief in God to everyday action.

bullets: God is just, so Jews are called to act fairly and stand up for the powerless.
Jews campaign against poverty, racism and unfair treatment, and for fair pay and human rights.
Amos 5:24: 'Let justice roll down like water'.
**Tikkun Olam** means repairing the world: caring for people, animals and the environment.
Rabbi Tarfon taught: 'It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to neglect it' (Pirkei Avot 2:16, part of the Mishnah).
Examples: charity work, environmental projects, volunteering, working for peace.
Many Reform Jews see Tikkun Olam as a main way of living out their faith.
**Tzedakah** comes from the word for righteousness: giving is a duty, not just a kindness.
Jews are expected to give at least a tenth of income (**maaser**). Many homes have a tzedakah box.
Maimonides said the highest form of giving is helping a person become self-sufficient.
Wealth is seen as a loan from God to use well.
**Chesed** means loving-kindness: acts done freely from the heart.
The Talmud says chesed is greater than tzedakah, because it can be done for rich and poor, living and dead, with money or time.
'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18) and Rabbi Hillel's 'What is hateful to you, do not do to others' sum up the Torah.
Examples: visiting the sick, welcoming guests, comforting mourners.

**Justice**: 'Justice, justice shall you pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20). The Torah protects the poor, the widow, the orphan and the stranger (Deuteronomy 10:18, Leviticus 19:34) and demands fair wages and honest weights.

**Healing the world**: the phrase 'tikkun olam' comes from the Mishnah, where the rabbis made rules 'for the good order of the world', and from the Aleinu prayer, which hopes 'to repair the world under the sovereignty of God'.
**Charity**: 'Open your hand to the poor and needy' (Deuteronomy 15:11). Farmers had to leave the edges of fields and fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger (Leviticus 19:9-10).
**Kindness**: Pirkei Avot 1:2 says the world stands on three things: the Torah, worship and acts of loving-kindness (gemilut chasadim).
Maimonides listed eight levels of giving. The lowest is giving unwillingly.
Higher levels are giving before being asked and giving anonymously, so the poor person is not embarrassed.
The highest level is helping someone become **self-sufficient**, for example with a job, training or a business loan, so they no longer need charity.
AQA's 2026 sample mark scheme also accepts **saving a life** (Pikuach Nefesh) as a key moral principle, linked to the sanctity of life (see the next topic).
**Mitzvah Day**: a yearly day of social action when Jewish communities in the UK volunteer, often with people of other faiths, for example collecting for food banks or cleaning up parks.
Jewish charities such as **World Jewish Relief** (international aid and refugees) and **Jewish Care** (care for older and vulnerable people) put tzedakah and chesed into practice.
Many synagogues run food bank collections, visit the sick (bikur cholim) and welcome guests to Shabbat meals (hachnasat orchim).
Some Jews put coins in a tzedakah box before Shabbat starts, and give extra charity during the Days of Awe.

views.label: Orthodox
views.text: Justice, charity and kindness are mitzvot that come from the Torah and must be done as commands from God, alongside ritual mitzvot.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Place special emphasis on the ethical teachings of the prophets and on Tikkun Olam and social action as the heart of Judaism.

topics.title: Sanctity of life and Pikuach Nefesh
topics.overview: Jews believe all human life is holy because it comes from God. The duty to save life (Pikuach Nefesh) can override almost every other Jewish law.

bullets: Life is **sacred** because humans are created in God's image (Genesis 1:27) and life belongs to God.
The Mishnah says that saving one life is like saving a whole world (Sanhedrin 4:5).
Jews believe God knows each person before birth (Psalm 139), so every person has value, including the disabled and the elderly.
Deuteronomy 30:19 tells Jews to 'choose life'.
**Pikuach Nefesh** is the duty to save a life, even if it means breaking other laws.
A doctor can work on **Shabbat**, and Jews can break kosher rules or fast on Yom Kippur if life is at risk.
If it is unclear whether life is at risk, Jews assume it is.
There are exceptions: a Jew must not murder, commit idolatry, or commit forbidden sexual relations, even to save a life (Talmud, Sanhedrin 74a).
Many Jews support organ donation, because saving a life is more important than keeping the body whole.
Jews work in medicine and emergency services, and run charities such as Hatzolah volunteer ambulances.
Many Jews oppose euthanasia and are cautious about abortion, but allow it if the mother's life is at risk.
The rule comes from Leviticus 18:5: Jews should keep the laws and 'live by them'. The Talmud (Yoma 85b) adds 'and not die by them'.
The Mishnah (Yoma 8:6) teaches that even where it is only uncertain whether a life is in danger, Shabbat may be set aside.
Many rabbis teach that breaking a law to save a life is not just allowed but required, and that the person who acts quickest is the most praiseworthy.
The duty also applies to helping others: 'Do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour' (Leviticus 19:16).
No one may take one innocent life to save another, because every life has equal value. This is why murder is one of the three exceptions.

**Organ donation**: many rabbis encourage it as Pikuach Nefesh; some Orthodox Jews have concerns about how death is defined and consult a rabbi. Since 2020 England has an 'opt-out' organ donation system, and families can ask for faith beliefs to be respected.

**Abortion**: in Orthodox Judaism the mother's life comes first if her life is in danger (Mishnah Oholot 7:6), but abortion for other reasons is generally not allowed. Reform Jews tend to allow more room for the mother's wellbeing and conscience.

**Euthanasia**: actively ending a life is forbidden in Orthodox teaching, since life belongs to God. Some rabbis allow removing things that only prolong the dying process. Views among Reform Jews are more varied.
Treat the sanctity of **human** life as the focus of this topic. Animals must be treated kindly (tza'ar ba'alei chayim), but the sanctity of life teaching is about humans made in God's image.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Also value life as sacred, but give more weight to personal conscience and compassion in medical decisions. Views on end-of-life choices vary more widely than in Orthodox Judaism.

topics.title: Free will, the 613 mitzvot, and mitzvot between man and God and man and man
topics.overview: Jews believe God gave humans free will, and that they should use it to keep the 613 mitzvot. Orthodox and Reform Jews differ on how binding the mitzvot are.

bullets: Jews believe humans can choose between good and evil. Maimonides wrote: 'Free will is granted to every human being.'
Everyone has a good inclination (**yetzer ha-tov**) and a bad inclination (**yetzer ha-ra**) and must choose which to follow.
Free will matters because God judges people on their choices.
Pirkei Avot 3:15: 'Everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given.'
The Torah contains **613 mitzvot**: 248 positive commands ('do') and 365 negative commands ('do not').
Some are ritual mitzvot (such as Shabbat and kosher food), and some are ethical (such as justice and charity).
Mitzvot **between people and God** (bein adam la-Makom) include prayer, Shabbat and food laws. Mitzvot **between people** (bein adam le-chavero) include honouring parents and giving charity.
Both types are important. On Yom Kippur God forgives sins against God, but for sins against people you must first seek forgiveness from the person.
**Orthodox**: the mitzvot are God's commands and are binding. Free will means choosing to obey them.
**Reform**: Jews use informed free will to decide which mitzvot to keep, focusing on those with ethical or spiritual meaning.
This explains why Jews differ over Shabbat, kosher food, and prayer.
In Genesis 4:7 God warns Cain that sin is 'crouching at the door', but 'you can master it': humans can choose to resist wrongdoing.
Without free will, keeping the mitzvot would have no value and God's judgement would not be fair.

The yetzer ha-ra is not simply evil: the rabbis taught it also drives ambition and family life, and must be controlled, not destroyed. Studying Torah and keeping mitzvot help strengthen the yetzer ha-tov.
Free will explains why there is suffering caused by humans: God allows people to make real choices.

The Talmud (Makkot 23b) records Rabbi Simlai's teaching: 613 mitzvot were given to Moses, 365 'do not' commands (like the days of the year) and 248 'do' commands (traditionally linked to the parts of the body).
Not every Jew can keep all 613: many concern the Temple, the priests or farming in the land of Israel. Some apply only to men or only to women.
The mitzvot cover every part of life, so even ordinary acts like eating or getting dressed can become a way of serving God.

notes.h: Mitzvot between man and God and between man and man
bullets: AQA calls them mitzvot **between man and God** (bein adam la-Makom) and **between man and man** (bein adam le-chavero).
Between man and God: belief in one God, prayer, keeping Shabbat and festivals, food laws, not misusing God's name, wearing tefillin.
Between man and man: honouring parents, not stealing or lying, giving tzedakah, paying fair wages, visiting the sick, loving your neighbour (Leviticus 19:18).
The Ten Commandments contain both types. Leviticus 19 also mixes them, showing that holiness covers worship and how people are treated.
The Mishnah (Yoma 8:9) teaches that Yom Kippur atones for sins between a person and God, but sins against another person are not forgiven until the person has been appeased.
Rabbi Hillel summed up the Torah as 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; the rest is commentary, go and learn' (Talmud, Shabbat 31a).

Most Jews say both types are equally important because both come from God. Some argue that mitzvot between people show whether a person's worship is sincere, while others argue the mitzvot towards God are the foundation of all the rest.

notes.h: How these beliefs influence Jews today
bullets: Orthodox Jews follow halakhah (Jewish law) in detail, asking a rabbi when unsure, because the mitzvot are God's commands.
Keeping the mitzvot unites Jews and gives a shared identity, for example a fixed pattern of dress, worship and food in some communities.
Reform and Liberal Jews make informed choices, often keeping ethical mitzvot fully but some ritual laws (such as certain food laws) less strictly.
Before Yom Kippur Jews apologise to people they have hurt, showing the importance of mitzvot between people.

views.label: Reform
views.text: Jews have the autonomy to interpret the mitzvot. They choose those that give their lives meaning and help society, while ethical mitzvot are seen as central.

flashcards.q: What does monotheism mean?
flashcards.a: Belief in only one God. Jews believe in one God who is eternal, all-powerful, has no body and cannot be divided.

flashcards.q: What is the Shema and where is it from?
flashcards.a: The Jewish declaration of faith: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One' (Deuteronomy 6:4). Said morning and evening.

flashcards.q: What does 'ex nihilo' mean in Jewish belief about creation?
flashcards.a: God created the universe from nothing, which shows God's unlimited power.

flashcards.q: Which commandment forbids worshipping other gods?
flashcards.a: 'You shall have no other gods before Me' (Exodus 20:3). It supports the belief that God is One.

flashcards.q: How does Isaiah 45:7 show God as creator?
flashcards.a: It says God forms light and creates darkness. It shows God creates and keeps sustaining all things, not only at the start.

flashcards.q: How can belief in God as creator influence a Jew today?
flashcards.a: It encourages them to thank God, keep Shabbat, and look after the world as God's stewards (Psalm 24:1).

flashcards.q: How many mitzvot are in the Torah?
flashcards.a: 613: 248 positive commands (do) and 365 negative commands (do not).

flashcards.q: Which quote describes God as judge, lawgiver and king?
flashcards.a: Isaiah 33:22: 'For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king.'

flashcards.q: What does 'teshuvah' mean?
flashcards.a: Repentance, or 'returning' to God. God is merciful and forgives those who sincerely repent.

flashcards.q: When do Jews believe God judges people?
flashcards.a: Especially on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur each year, and after death.

flashcards.q: Which verse shows God is loving and merciful?
flashcards.a: Exodus 34:6: God is 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in kindness'.

flashcards.q: What are the Noahide laws?
flashcards.a: Seven basic laws God gave to Noah for all humanity, such as not murdering or stealing.

flashcards.q: What does Shekhinah mean?
flashcards.a: The divine presence of God: God cannot be seen, but God's presence can be felt in the world.

flashcards.q: Give two examples of the Shekhinah in the Tenakh.
flashcards.a: The burning bush (Exodus 3) and the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21).

flashcards.q: Where does the word Shekhinah come from?
flashcards.a: It is not in the Tenakh itself. The rabbis use it in the Talmud and Midrash. It is a feminine Hebrew word.

flashcards.q: What does Pirkei Avot 3:6 say about the Shekhinah?
flashcards.a: When ten sit together studying Torah, the Shekhinah is among them. This links to the minyan.

flashcards.q: What is a minyan?
flashcards.a: Ten adults needed for communal prayer. Orthodox count men only. Reform count men and women.

flashcards.q: How does belief in the Shekhinah help Jews today?
flashcards.a: It gives comfort in suffering: God is close and never abandons them, even in exile.

flashcards.q: What is Olam Ha-Ba?
flashcards.a: 'The world to come': the afterlife or future age where the righteous are with God.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between Gan Eden and Gehinnom?
flashcards.a: Gan Eden is paradise for the righteous. Gehinnom is a place of purification, not usually eternal punishment.

flashcards.q: What do many Orthodox Jews believe about resurrection?
flashcards.a: That God will physically raise the dead at the end of time. This is why they bury and do not cremate.

flashcards.q: What do many Reform Jews believe about the afterlife?
flashcards.a: That the soul is immortal, not that the body is physically resurrected. Some accept cremation.

flashcards.q: What is gilgul?
flashcards.a: Reincarnation: some Kabbalists and Hasidic Jews believe souls return to complete mitzvot and help heal the world.

flashcards.q: Which verse in Daniel supports judgement and resurrection?
flashcards.a: Daniel 12:2: 'Many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, others to shame.'

flashcards.q: What does Messiah mean?
flashcards.a: 'Anointed one' (Mashiach in Hebrew). It refers to a future leader sent by God.

flashcards.q: Who will the Messiah be descended from?
flashcards.a: King David (Jeremiah 23:5).

flashcards.q: What is the Messianic Age?
flashcards.a: A future age of world peace and justice, with no war or hunger, when everyone worships the One God.

flashcards.q: How do Orthodox and Reform views of the Messiah differ?
flashcards.a: Orthodox expect a personal Messiah who rebuilds the Temple. Reform expect no person but a Messianic Age brought by human effort.

flashcards.q: Which Maimonides principle is about the Messiah?
flashcards.a: The 12th: belief in the coming of the Messiah, even if he is delayed.

flashcards.q: How does belief in the Messiah influence Jews today?
flashcards.a: It gives hope in hard times and encourages them to keep the mitzvot or work for justice and peace (Tikkun Olam).

flashcards.q: What three things did God promise Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3?
flashcards.a: A great nation (many descendants), a blessing, and a land (Canaan).

flashcards.q: What was the sign of the covenant with Abraham?
flashcards.a: Circumcision of every male (Genesis 17:10-11), done on the eighth day as Brit Milah.

flashcards.q: What name changes happened in the covenant with Abraham?
flashcards.a: Abram became Abraham and Sarai became Sarah.

flashcards.q: What is aliyah?
flashcards.a: 'Going up': moving to Israel. It also means being called up to read from the Torah.

flashcards.q: What does 'chosen people' mean for Jews?
flashcards.a: God chose the Jews for a special relationship and duty to keep the mitzvot. It is a responsibility, not a privilege.

flashcards.q: Which story tests Abraham's faith?
flashcards.a: Genesis 22: God asks Abraham to sacrifice Isaac, then provides a ram instead. It shows Abraham's faith, but it is not part of the covenant itself.

flashcards.q: Where did God give the Ten Commandments to Moses?
flashcards.a: On Mount Sinai (Exodus 19-20).

flashcards.q: What was the sign of the covenant with Moses?
flashcards.a: Shabbat (Exodus 31:16-17).

flashcards.q: Which Ten Commandments are about people and God?
flashcards.a: One God, no idols, do not misuse God's name and keep Shabbat.

flashcards.q: How did the Israelites respond at Sinai?
flashcards.a: 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exodus 24:7).

flashcards.q: What does Judaism count as the first commandment?
flashcards.a: 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt' (Exodus 20:2).

flashcards.q: Name two commandments between people and people.
flashcards.a: Honour your parents, and do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie about others or covet.

flashcards.q: What is Tikkun Olam?
flashcards.a: 'Healing the world': caring for people, animals and the environment to make the world better.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between tzedakah and chesed?
flashcards.a: Tzedakah is giving charity as a duty. Chesed is loving-kindness shown freely to anyone, rich or poor, with money or acts.

flashcards.q: What is maaser?
flashcards.a: Giving a tenth of income to charity.

flashcards.q: Quote Amos 5:24 on justice.
flashcards.a: 'Let justice roll on like a river, righteousness like a never-failing stream.'

flashcards.q: What did Maimonides say is the highest form of giving?
flashcards.a: Helping a person become self-sufficient, for example by giving them a job or loan.

flashcards.q: Which verse is often used for kindness to others?
flashcards.a: Leviticus 19:18: 'Love your neighbour as yourself.'

flashcards.q: What does Pikuach Nefesh mean?
flashcards.a: Saving a life: the duty to save life overrides almost all other Jewish laws.

flashcards.q: Which three laws can never be broken to save a life?
flashcards.a: Murder, idolatry, and forbidden sexual relations (Sanhedrin 74a).

flashcards.q: Why is human life sacred in Judaism?
flashcards.a: Humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) and life belongs to God.

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teach?
flashcards.a: Saving one life is like saving a whole world.

flashcards.q: Give an example of Pikuach Nefesh on Shabbat.
flashcards.a: A Jewish doctor working on Shabbat to treat an emergency, or driving someone to hospital.

flashcards.q: How does sanctity of life influence Jews' views on organ donation?
flashcards.a: Many Jews support it as saving life is a mitzvah that outweighs keeping the body intact.

flashcards.q: What is free will?
flashcards.a: The ability to choose between right and wrong and to be responsible for the choice.

flashcards.q: How many positive and negative mitzvot are there?
flashcards.a: 248 positive (do) and 365 negative (do not): 613 in total.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between mitzvot between people and God, and between people?
flashcards.a: Between people and God: prayer, Shabbat, food laws. Between people: honour parents, give charity, do not steal.

flashcards.q: What are the yetzer ha-tov and yetzer ha-ra?
flashcards.a: The good and bad inclinations in every person. Free will means choosing which to follow.

flashcards.q: How do Orthodox and Reform Jews differ on the mitzvot?
flashcards.a: Orthodox treat all as binding commands. Reform use informed free will to choose which to keep.

flashcards.q: What does Pirkei Avot 3:15 say?
flashcards.a: 'Everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given.'

flashcards.q: What does the rest of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5-7) command?
flashcards.a: To love God with all your heart, soul and might, to keep God's words in your heart and to teach them to your children.

flashcards.q: Why are there no pictures or statues of God in a synagogue?
flashcards.a: God has no body or form, and the commandments forbid making idols (Exodus 20:4). Any image would be idolatry.

flashcards.q: Which festival do the rabbis link to the creation of the world?
flashcards.a: Rosh Hashanah, often called the 'birthday of the world'.

flashcards.q: Complete the quote: 'The earth is the Lord's...' (Psalm 24:1)
flashcards.a: '...and everything in it, the world and all who live in it.' Used for stewardship.

flashcards.q: What do transcendent and immanent mean?
flashcards.a: Transcendent: God is beyond and greater than the universe. Immanent: God is close to and involved in the world.

flashcards.q: What happens on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, according to tradition?
flashcards.a: On Rosh Hashanah God writes each person's fate for the year in the books of judgement; on Yom Kippur the judgement is sealed.

flashcards.q: What must a Jew do before Yom Kippur if they have wronged another person?
flashcards.a: Ask that person for forgiveness and put things right. God forgives sins against God, but not sins against people until the person is reconciled.

flashcards.q: What does Ezekiel 18:23 show about God?
flashcards.a: God does not want the wicked to die but to turn from their ways and live: God is merciful and wants repentance.

flashcards.q: Why can God be both Judge and merciful?
flashcards.a: God judges fairly but wants people to change. Sincere teshuvah (repentance) leads to forgiveness (Exodus 34:6).

flashcards.q: What happened when the Tabernacle was completed (Exodus 40:34)?
flashcards.a: A cloud covered it and the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle: an example of the Shekhinah.

flashcards.q: Why is the Western Wall linked to the Shekhinah?
flashcards.a: Tradition says the divine presence never left the Western Wall, the last remaining part of the Temple compound, so Jews pray there.

flashcards.q: Which synagogue feature is often linked to God's constant presence?
flashcards.a: The ner tamid, the ever-burning light above the ark.

flashcards.q: What does Berakhot 6a in the Talmud teach about prayer?
flashcards.a: When ten people pray together, the divine presence is with them: the basis for valuing the minyan.

flashcards.q: What three groups does the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 16b) describe at judgement?
flashcards.a: The wholly righteous, the wholly wicked, and the in-between (most people), who have time to repent.

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 teach about the world to come?
flashcards.a: 'All Israel have a share in the world to come.' Maimonides adds that the righteous of all nations have a share too.

flashcards.q: What did the Reform Pittsburgh Platform (1885) say about life after death?
flashcards.a: The soul is immortal, but it rejected bodily resurrection and Gehenna and Eden as places of eternal punishment and reward.

flashcards.q: Why do many Orthodox Jews not allow cremation?
flashcards.a: They believe in bodily resurrection and that the body was created by God and should be buried whole and with respect.

flashcards.q: Is the Messiah divine in Jewish belief?
flashcards.a: No. The Messiah is a human being chosen by God, not God and not a saviour from sin.

flashcards.q: Name four tasks Jews believe the Messiah will carry out.
flashcards.a: Rule as a just king from David's line, gather the exiles to Israel, rebuild the Temple, bring world peace and lead all people to know God.

flashcards.q: Why do Jews not accept Jesus as the Messiah?
flashcards.a: The Messianic tasks have not happened: there is no world peace, the Temple has not been rebuilt and the exiles have not been gathered.

flashcards.q: What did the Reform Pittsburgh Platform (1885) say about the Messiah?
flashcards.a: It spoke of the Messianic hope as an age of truth, justice and peace for all people, not a personal king restoring a Jewish state.

flashcards.q: What did God tell Abram to do in Genesis 12:1?
flashcards.a: Leave his country, his people and his father's house and go to the land God would show him.

flashcards.q: What does the name Abraham mean?
flashcards.a: 'Father of many nations' (from Genesis 17:5), given when God confirmed the covenant.

flashcards.q: What does 'chosen people' NOT mean?
flashcards.a: It does not mean Jews are better than others. It means chosen for responsibility: to keep the mitzvot and be a light to the nations.

flashcards.q: Which son of Abraham continued the covenant?
flashcards.a: Isaac, born to Sarah in her old age; then Isaac's son Jacob (Israel).

flashcards.q: Give three key events in the life of Moses.
flashcards.a: The burning bush (call by God), leading the Exodus from Egypt, receiving the Torah and Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai (also: the plagues, the golden calf, 40 years in the wilderness).

flashcards.q: What does Deuteronomy 34:10 say about Moses?
flashcards.a: No prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face.

flashcards.q: Which festival celebrates the giving of the Torah at Sinai?
flashcards.a: Shavuot.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between Orthodox and Reform views of the Torah given at Sinai?
flashcards.a: Orthodox: given word for word by God to Moses (Torah from heaven). Reform: inspired by God but written by humans, so open to reinterpretation.

flashcards.q: What does Deuteronomy 16:20 command?
flashcards.a: 'Justice, justice shall you pursue': Jews must actively work for justice.

flashcards.q: What is the lowest level on Maimonides' ladder of tzedakah?
flashcards.a: Giving unwillingly or grudgingly. The highest is helping someone become self-sufficient.

flashcards.q: What are the three things the world stands on (Pirkei Avot 1:2)?
flashcards.a: The Torah, worship (avodah) and acts of loving-kindness (gemilut chasadim).

flashcards.q: Where does the phrase 'tikkun olam' come from?
flashcards.a: The Mishnah (rules made for the good order of the world) and the Aleinu prayer ('to repair the world under the sovereignty of God').

flashcards.q: Name two UK Jewish organisations that put moral principles into action.
flashcards.a: Mitzvah Day, World Jewish Relief, Jewish Care (any two).

flashcards.q: Which verse is the basis of Pikuach Nefesh, and how does the Talmud explain it?
flashcards.a: Leviticus 18:5: keep the laws and 'live by them'. The Talmud (Yoma 85b) adds 'and not die by them'.

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Oholot 7:6 teach about a mother whose life is at risk in childbirth?
flashcards.a: Her life comes first before the unborn child's, until most of the baby has been born.

flashcards.q: What does Leviticus 19:16 command?
flashcards.a: 'Do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour': Jews must act to save others.

flashcards.q: What do many Orthodox rabbis teach about euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Actively ending a life is forbidden because life belongs to God, though some allow removing things that only prolong dying.

flashcards.q: What is Hatzolah?
flashcards.a: A Jewish volunteer emergency ambulance service that runs in some UK cities, including on Shabbat, as an act of Pikuach Nefesh.

flashcards.q: What does the Talmud (Makkot 23b) say about the 613 mitzvot?
flashcards.a: Rabbi Simlai taught 613 were given to Moses: 365 negative (like days of the year) and 248 positive (like the parts of the body).

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Yoma 8:9 teach about Yom Kippur?
flashcards.a: It atones for sins between a person and God, but sins against another person are only forgiven once that person has been appeased.

flashcards.q: How did Hillel sum up the Torah (Shabbat 31a)?
flashcards.a: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; the rest is commentary, go and learn.'

flashcards.q: Why can no one keep all 613 mitzvot today?
flashcards.a: Many relate to the Temple, priests or farming in Israel, and some apply only to men or only to women.

flashcards.q: What does Genesis 4:7 show about free will?
flashcards.a: God tells Cain sin is crouching at the door but 'you can master it': humans can choose to resist wrongdoing.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the Jewish declaration of faith that God is One?
quiz.why: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) states that the Lord is One. It is said morning and evening.

quiz.q: Which one of the following best describes 'ex nihilo'?
options: God created the world in seven days
quiz.why: Ex nihilo means 'from nothing': most Jews believe God made the universe from nothing, showing God's power.

quiz.q: Why do Jews reject the Christian idea of the Trinity?
options: They believe God is indivisible and One
They believe God is not creator
They believe God has a body
They do not believe in prayer
quiz.why: Jews believe God is a single, indivisible One (the Shema), so God cannot be three persons.

quiz.q: How many mitzvot (commandments) are there in the Torah?
quiz.why: The Torah contains 613 mitzvot: 248 positive and 365 negative (Talmud, Makkot 23b). Do not confuse the total with the two separate figures.

quiz.q: Isaiah 33:22 describes God as which of the following?
quiz.why: Isaiah 33:22 says 'The Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king'.

quiz.q: A Jew says God is both just and merciful. Which belief about God does this show?
options: God is judge and loving and merciful
God is not involved in the world
quiz.why: AQA lists God as Law-Giver and Judge, loving and merciful: God judges fairly but forgives those who truly repent.

quiz.q: Which one of the following terms means the divine presence of God?
quiz.why: Shekhinah means God's presence felt in the world.

quiz.q: Which one of these is an example of the Shekhinah in the Tenakh?
options: The pillar of cloud and fire
quiz.why: Exodus 13:21 describes God going before the Israelites in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.

quiz.q: How might belief in the Shekhinah influence a Jew who is suffering?
options: It reminds them God is with them and does not abandon them
It tells them God is absent
It tells them to leave Judaism
It means they do not need to pray
quiz.why: The rabbis taught that the Shekhinah went into exile with the Jews, which gives comfort.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the place of purification in Jewish belief about the afterlife?
quiz.why: Gehinnom is usually seen as a place of purification. Gan Eden is paradise, and Olam Ha-Zeh is this world.

quiz.q: Why do many Orthodox Jews bury their dead and not cremate?
options: They do not believe in an afterlife
They believe in a physical resurrection of the body
quiz.why: Orthodox Jews believe God will physically raise the dead, so the body is buried.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the belief of many Reform Jews?
options: There is no afterlife of any kind
quiz.why: Many Reform Jews believe in the immortality of the soul rather than a physical resurrection.

quiz.q: What does the word Messiah mean?
quiz.why: Mashiach means 'anointed one' because kings were anointed with oil.

quiz.q: Which one of the following do many Orthodox Jews believe about the Messiah?
options: He has already come as Jesus
He will be a descendant of King David
quiz.why: Jeremiah 23:5 says the Messiah will come from David's line. Jews do not believe Jesus was the Messiah.

quiz.q: A Reform Jew believes the Messianic Age will come through human effort. How might this influence them?
options: They work for justice and peace (Tikkun Olam)
quiz.why: If the Messianic Age depends on humans, Reform Jews are influenced to work for a better world.

quiz.q: Which one of the following was the sign of the covenant with Abraham?
quiz.why: Genesis 17:10-11 says circumcision is the sign of the covenant with Abraham.

quiz.q: Which one of these did God NOT promise Abraham in Genesis 12:1-3?
quiz.why: God promised nation, blessing and land. The Temple was built much later by Solomon.

quiz.q: A Jewish family emigrates to Israel. What is this called?
quiz.why: Aliyah means 'going up': moving to Israel.

quiz.q: Where did Moses receive the Ten Commandments?
quiz.why: God gave the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19-20).

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the sign of the covenant with Moses?
quiz.why: Exodus 31:16-17 says Shabbat is a lasting sign of the covenant with Israel.

quiz.q: Which one of these is a commandment between people and people?
quiz.why: 'You shall not murder' is about how people treat each other. The others are about the relationship with God.

quiz.q: Which one of the following means 'healing the world'?
quiz.why: Tikkun Olam means healing or repairing the world.

quiz.q: According to the Talmud, why is chesed greater than tzedakah?
options: It is in the Ten Commandments
It can be done for rich and poor, living and dead, with money or acts
quiz.why: The Talmud (Sukkah 49b) says chesed can be done for anyone and in any way.

quiz.q: A Jewish family always puts aside a tenth of their income for charity. What is this called?
quiz.why: Maaser means giving a tenth of income, a form of tzedakah.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is Pikuach Nefesh?
quiz.why: Pikuach Nefesh means saving a life, which overrides almost all other laws.

quiz.q: A Jewish doctor is called to work on Shabbat for an emergency. What belief allows this?
quiz.why: Pikuach Nefesh allows work on Shabbat to save life.

quiz.q: Which one of these laws may NOT be broken to save a life?
quiz.why: The Talmud says murder, idolatry and forbidden sexual relations may never be broken, even to save a life.

quiz.q: How many negative mitzvot ('do not') are there?
quiz.why: There are 365 negative and 248 positive mitzvot, making 613.

quiz.q: Which one of the following best describes the Reform view of the mitzvot?
options: All are binding in the same way
Jews use informed free will to choose which to follow
quiz.why: Reform Jews see mitzvot as guidance and use informed choice, while Orthodox Jews treat them as binding.

quiz.q: Which one of these is a mitzvah between people and God?
quiz.why: Shabbat is between people and God. The other options are between people.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is placed on the doorposts of a Jewish home and contains the Shema?
quiz.why: The mezuzah is a small parchment scroll with the Shema written on it, fixed to doorposts as Deuteronomy 6:9 commands.

quiz.q: A Jewish family plants trees at Tu B'Shevat and recycles carefully. Which belief does this mainly show?
options: God as Creator, so humans are stewards
quiz.why: Because God created the world and 'the earth is the Lord's' (Psalm 24:1), Jews have a duty to look after it.

quiz.q: Which word means that God is beyond and outside the universe?
quiz.why: Transcendent means beyond the universe. Immanent means close and involved; omniscient means all-knowing.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is the odd one out as a way Jews show belief that God is One?
options: Saying the Shema twice a day
Refusing to make images of God
Fixing a mezuzah to the door
quiz.why: The Trinity is a Christian belief. Jews reject it because God is One and indivisible.

quiz.q: Which period is a time for repentance between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur?
quiz.why: The ten Days of Awe run from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, when Jews repent before judgement is sealed.

quiz.q: Which source best supports the belief that God is merciful?
quiz.why: Exodus 34:6 describes God as 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in kindness'.

quiz.q: A Jew phones a friend they upset to apologise before Yom Kippur. Which belief does this show?
options: God forgives sins against others only after the person is reconciled
Sins against people do not matter
quiz.why: On Yom Kippur God forgives sins against God, but sins against people need the person's forgiveness first (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

quiz.q: Which source says the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle?
quiz.why: Exodus 40:34 describes the cloud covering the Tent of Meeting and God's glory filling the Tabernacle.

quiz.q: Where do many Jews believe the Shekhinah never left?
quiz.why: A rabbinic tradition says the divine presence never left the Western Wall of the Temple compound.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Shekhinah is correct?
options: It is the felt presence of the one God
It is a word found many times in the Torah
It is the name of the Temple
quiz.why: The Shekhinah is the divine presence of the one God, a rabbinic term not found in the Tenakh itself.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is NOT a Jewish term connected with life after death?
quiz.why: Purgatory is a Catholic Christian idea. Gan Eden, Olam Ha-Ba and Sheol are Jewish terms.

quiz.q: Which source teaches that only Torah and good deeds go with a person when they die?
quiz.why: Pirkei Avot 6:9 says neither silver nor gold goes with a person at death, only Torah and good deeds.

quiz.q: A Jewish family chooses cremation for a relative who believed in the immortality of the soul. Which tradition is most likely to accept this?
quiz.why: Many Reform Jews believe in the soul's immortality rather than physical resurrection, so some accept cremation. Orthodox and Hasidic Jews require burial.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a traditional Jewish belief about the Messiah?
options: He will die to save people from sin
He will be descended from David
quiz.why: Dying for sins is a Christian belief about Jesus. The Jewish Messiah is a human king and teacher.

quiz.q: 'The wolf shall dwell with the lamb' describes the Messianic Age. Where is this found?
quiz.why: Isaiah 11:6 pictures a world of complete peace in the Messianic Age.

quiz.q: A Jew says 'We should not wait for one person; we must build a better world together.' Which view is this closest to?
options: A Reform view of a Messianic Age
quiz.why: Many Reform Jews hope for a Messianic Age brought about by human effort, rather than a personal Messiah.

quiz.q: Which passage does AQA name for the covenant with Abraham?
quiz.why: The specification names Genesis 12:1-3 for the Promised Land and the covenant with Abraham.

quiz.q: Which one of these is NOT part of the covenant with Abraham?
quiz.why: The Ten Commandments belong to the covenant at Sinai with Moses.

quiz.q: In which book and chapter is circumcision given as the sign of the covenant?
quiz.why: Genesis 17:10-11 commands circumcision of every male as the sign of the covenant.

quiz.q: Which festival celebrates the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai?
quiz.why: Shavuot marks the giving of the Torah; the Ten Commandments are read in synagogue.

quiz.q: What did Moses do when he saw the people worshipping the golden calf?
quiz.why: Moses broke the first tablets, then prayed for the people and received a second set (Exodus 32 to 34).

quiz.q: In the Jewish numbering, which commandment is 'Remember Shabbat and keep it holy'?
quiz.why: It is the fourth commandment in Jewish numbering (Exodus 20:8).

quiz.q: Which one of the following is NOT one of the key moral principles named in the specification?
quiz.why: The key moral principles are justice, healing the world, charity and kindness to others. Waiting for the Messiah is a belief, not a moral principle.

quiz.q: According to Maimonides, what is the highest form of tzedakah?
options: Giving to your own family only
quiz.why: The top of Maimonides' ladder is helping a person support themselves, for example with work or a loan.

quiz.q: Which prayer, said at the end of services, hopes 'to repair the world' under God's rule?
quiz.why: The Aleinu prayer contains the phrase linked to tikkun olam.

quiz.q: Which source says Jews should 'live by' the laws, the basis of Pikuach Nefesh?
quiz.why: Leviticus 18:5 says to keep God's laws and live by them; the Talmud adds 'not die by them'.

quiz.q: A Jewish teenager is unsure whether a friend's illness is life-threatening on Shabbat. What should they do according to Jewish law?
options: Ask a rabbi first, however long it takes
Treat it as life-threatening and get help
Do nothing because it is Shabbat
quiz.why: Where there is doubt about danger to life, Shabbat is set aside (Mishnah Yoma 8:6).

quiz.q: Why is murder one of the exceptions to Pikuach Nefesh?
options: Because no one may take one innocent life to save another
Because the Ten Commandments do not mention it
quiz.why: Every life is equally sacred, so you cannot kill an innocent person even to save your own life.

quiz.q: Which of these is a mitzvah between man and man?
quiz.why: Paying fair wages promptly (Leviticus 19:13) concerns how people treat each other.

quiz.q: Which source teaches that Yom Kippur does not atone for sins against other people until they are appeased?
quiz.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 makes the distinction between sins against God and sins against people.

quiz.q: What is the Hebrew name for the good inclination?
quiz.why: The yetzer ha-tov is the good inclination; the yetzer ha-ra is the inclination to do wrong.

truefalse.s: Jews believe God has no body or physical form.
truefalse.why: God is spirit, not physical. This is one of Maimonides' principles and is why Jews make no images of God.

truefalse.s: The Shema is found in the book of Genesis.
truefalse.why: The Shema is Deuteronomy 6:4-9. Genesis 1 contains the creation account.

truefalse.s: Shabbat reminds Jews that God rested on the seventh day of creation.
truefalse.why: Genesis 2:2-3 and the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:8-11) link Shabbat to creation.

truefalse.s: All Jews read Genesis 1 as a literal scientific account of creation.
truefalse.why: Many Orthodox Jews read it as a true account, but many Reform Jews accept science and read Genesis as teaching about God's purpose.

truefalse.s: Jews believe God continues to sustain the world after creating it.
truefalse.why: God is believed to keep creation going every day, not just to have started it (for example Isaiah 45:7).

truefalse.s: Jews believe God gave laws to all humanity through Noah, not only to Jews.
truefalse.why: The seven Noahide laws are believed to apply to all people; the 613 mitzvot are for Jews.

truefalse.s: In Judaism, God's judgement is only about life after death.
truefalse.why: Jews also believe God judges each year at Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, as well as after death.

truefalse.s: Teshuvah means repentance, or 'returning' to God.
truefalse.why: Teshuvah is turning back to God and changing behaviour, which God responds to with mercy.

truefalse.s: Jews believe God's judgement and God's mercy contradict each other.
truefalse.why: Jews see them as working together: God judges fairly but forgives those who sincerely repent (Exodus 34:6).

truefalse.s: Isaiah 33:22 describes God as judge, lawgiver and king.
truefalse.why: It says 'the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king'.

truefalse.s: The word Shekhinah appears many times in the Torah.
truefalse.why: The idea is in the Tenakh (cloud, fire, glory) but the word itself comes from the rabbis in the Talmud and Midrash.

truefalse.s: Jews believe the Shekhinah can be present when people study Torah together.
truefalse.why: Pirkei Avot 3:6 says when ten sit and study Torah, the Shekhinah is among them.

truefalse.s: The Shekhinah is a separate being from God.
truefalse.why: It is the presence of the one God, not a separate being; Judaism is strictly monotheistic.

truefalse.s: The pillar of cloud and fire that guided the Israelites is seen as an example of the Shekhinah.
truefalse.why: Exodus 13:21 describes God going before the people in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night.

truefalse.s: The Shekhinah is often described in feminine, motherly terms.
truefalse.why: Shekhinah is a feminine Hebrew noun, and tradition pictures it caring for and suffering with the people.

truefalse.s: Gehinnom is a place of eternal punishment for most people.
truefalse.why: Gehinnom is usually seen as a place of cleansing, traditionally for no more than 12 months, before the soul enters Gan Eden.

truefalse.s: The Tenakh says relatively little about life after death.
truefalse.why: It focuses on life now; ideas like resurrection appear only in a few later books such as Daniel 12:2.

truefalse.s: Maimonides' 13 Principles of Faith include belief in the resurrection of the dead.
truefalse.why: The 13th principle is belief that God will bring the dead back to life.

truefalse.s: Jews believe only Jewish people can have a share in the world to come.
truefalse.why: Maimonides taught that the righteous of all nations have a share in the world to come.

truefalse.s: Some Jews believe in gilgul, the return of the soul in another life.
truefalse.why: Some Kabbalist and Hasidic Jews believe a soul can return to complete mitzvot it did not fulfil.

truefalse.s: Jews believe the Messiah will be God in human form.
truefalse.why: The Jewish Messiah is a human leader anointed by God, not divine.

truefalse.s: Belief in the coming of the Messiah is one of Maimonides' 13 Principles of Faith.
truefalse.why: The 12th principle is belief in the coming of the Messiah.

truefalse.s: Many Reform Jews expect a personal Messiah who will rebuild the Temple.
truefalse.why: Many Reform Jews hope for a Messianic Age of peace brought by human effort rather than a personal Messiah.

truefalse.s: Mashiach means 'anointed one'.
truefalse.why: Kings of Israel were anointed with oil; the Messiah is a future anointed king.

truefalse.s: Jews believe the Messiah will judge the dead at the end of time.
truefalse.why: In Judaism God alone is the Judge. This confusion with Christian belief was noted by examiners.

truefalse.s: Genesis 12:1-3 includes the promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham.
truefalse.why: Genesis 12:3 ends with this promise, which Jews link to being a light to the nations.

truefalse.s: The binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) is the sign of the covenant with Abraham.
truefalse.why: The sign is circumcision (Genesis 17). The binding of Isaac tests Abraham's faith but is not part of the covenant.

truefalse.s: Being God's 'chosen people' is seen by Jews as a responsibility rather than a privilege.
truefalse.why: Jews are chosen to keep the mitzvot and set an example, not because they are superior.

truefalse.s: Abraham was originally called Abram.
truefalse.why: God changed his name to Abraham, 'father of many nations', in Genesis 17:5.

truefalse.s: All Jews believe they must move to Israel to keep the covenant.
truefalse.why: Some see aliyah as a mitzvah, but many Jews believe they can live a full Jewish life in other countries such as Britain.

truefalse.s: Moses led the Israelites into the Promised Land himself.
truefalse.why: Moses died before the Israelites entered the land; Joshua led them in (Deuteronomy 34).

truefalse.s: The Ten Commandments are part of the 613 mitzvot.
truefalse.why: They are included in the 613 commandments of the Torah.

truefalse.s: The covenant at Sinai was made with the whole people of Israel, not just one family.
truefalse.why: All the people agreed, 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exodus 24:7).

truefalse.s: Circumcision is one of the Ten Commandments.
truefalse.why: Circumcision is the sign of the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17), not one of the Ten Commandments.

truefalse.s: Judaism counts 'I am the Lord your God who brought you out of Egypt' as the first commandment.
truefalse.why: In Jewish tradition this statement of who God is counts as the first of the ten.

truefalse.s: Tzedakah comes from the Hebrew word for righteousness or justice.
truefalse.why: Tzedakah is linked to tzedek (justice), so giving is a duty of justice, not an optional extra.

truefalse.s: In Judaism, charity is only for other Jews.
truefalse.why: The Torah commands care for the stranger (Leviticus 19:34), and Jewish charities help people of all backgrounds.

truefalse.s: Giving anonymously is ranked higher than giving publicly on Maimonides' ladder.
truefalse.why: Anonymous giving protects the dignity of the person receiving help.

truefalse.s: Chesed can only be shown by giving money.
truefalse.why: Chesed includes acts like visiting the sick, comforting mourners and welcoming guests; the Talmud says it can be done with money or with oneself.

truefalse.s: Many Reform Jews see Tikkun Olam and social action as central to their Judaism.
truefalse.why: Reform Judaism stresses the ethical teaching of the prophets and social justice.

truefalse.s: Under Pikuach Nefesh, a Jew may eat non-kosher food if it is needed to save their life.
truefalse.why: Saving life overrides almost all mitzvot, including food laws.

truefalse.s: Pikuach Nefesh allows a Jew to murder someone if it saves their own life.
truefalse.why: Murder, idolatry and forbidden sexual relations may never be committed, even to save a life (Sanhedrin 74a).

truefalse.s: The sanctity of life teaching is mainly about human beings being made in God's image.
truefalse.why: Genesis 1:27 is the basis: humans reflect God, so human life is holy. Examiners noted answers about animals lost marks.

truefalse.s: Jews must be certain a life is in danger before breaking Shabbat.
truefalse.why: Even if there is only doubt, Shabbat is set aside to save life (Mishnah Yoma 8:6).

truefalse.s: The Mishnah says that saving one life is like saving a whole world.
truefalse.why: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches this, based on Adam being created as one person.

truefalse.s: There are 248 negative mitzvot in the Torah.
truefalse.why: There are 365 negative ('do not') and 248 positive ('do') mitzvot.

truefalse.s: Jews believe that without free will, keeping the mitzvot would not be meaningful.
truefalse.why: Obedience only has value if it is freely chosen, and God's judgement is fair only if people choose.

truefalse.s: Keeping Shabbat is a mitzvah between man and God.
truefalse.why: Shabbat concerns the relationship with God (rest and worship), though it also benefits family life.

truefalse.s: The yetzer ha-ra is a devil or evil spirit outside the person.
truefalse.why: It is an inclination within every person, which can be controlled and even used for good.

truefalse.s: The Ten Commandments include both mitzvot between man and God and between man and man.
truefalse.why: The first commandments concern God; the later ones (do not murder, steal, lie) concern other people.
