exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in God as Creator influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe God created the world and is still sustaining it. This influences Jews to thank God daily, for example by saying blessings before and after meals and praying the Shema each morning and evening.

Another way is that Jews believe God made the world and gave humans stewardship of it. This influences Jews to look after the environment, for example by recycling, planting trees or supporting conservation, because the earth belongs to God.
points: God as sole creator and sustainer: influences daily prayer, blessings and thanksgiving
Genesis 1 / Isaiah 45:7: creation has a purpose, so life has meaning
Stewardship (Psalm 24:1): influences care for the environment and animals (Tikkun Olam)
Shabbat remembers God resting after creation: influences keeping Shabbat
Humans made in God's image: influences respect for all people
Each way: 1 mark for the belief and 1 mark for how it influences Jews

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in God as Law-Giver and Judge influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe God gave the 613 mitzvot to guide how people live. This influences Jews to study the Torah and follow the mitzvot, for example keeping kosher food laws and Shabbat, because they believe this is what God wants.

Another way is that Jews believe God is a fair judge who judges people on Rosh Hashanah and after death. This influences Jews to behave well and treat others fairly, and to repent on Yom Kippur so that God will forgive them.
points: God gave the law at Sinai (613 mitzvot): influences obedience, study and practice (Orthodox strictly, Reform selectively)
God as judge: influences honest, fair and charitable living
Judgement at Rosh Hashanah/Yom Kippur: influences repentance (teshuvah) and seeking forgiveness
God is also merciful (Exodus 34:6): influences hope and willingness to change
Each way: 1 mark for the belief and 1 mark for how it influences Jews

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the Shekhinah influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe the Shekhinah is God's presence felt in the world. This influences Jews to feel that God is close to them in difficult times, such as illness or grief, so they pray and trust in God for comfort.

Another way is that the rabbis taught that the Shekhinah is present when ten people pray or study Torah together. This influences Jews to attend synagogue and to form a minyan so that they can worship as a community.
points: Shekhinah as God's presence felt but not seen: comfort and trust in hard times
Shekhinah went into exile with the Jews: God does not abandon them
Presence in a minyan or Torah study (Pirkei Avot 3:6): influences regular synagogue attendance and study
Examples (burning bush, pillar of fire): reinforce that God is active in the world
Each way: 1 mark for the belief and 1 mark for how it influences Jews

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the Messiah influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Orthodox Jews believe a Messiah from the line of King David will come and bring peace. This influences them to keep the mitzvot carefully and pray for his coming three times a day in the Amidah, because they believe this prepares the world for him.

Another way is that Reform Jews believe in a Messianic Age that humans help create. This influences them to work for justice and peace, for example through charity work and campaigning, to make the world better.
points: Orthodox: personal Messiah; influences prayer (Amidah) and strict mitzvot observance
Hope in suffering and persecution
Reform: Messianic Age through human effort; influences Tikkun Olam, justice and peace work
Messiah as peace-bringer (Isaiah 2:4): inspires Jews to seek peace
Each way: 1 mark for the belief and 1 mark for how it influences Jews

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in charity influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe tzedakah is a duty to God and not an optional extra. This influences many Jews to give a tenth of their income to charity and to keep a tzedakah box at home.

Another way is that Jews believe wealth is a loan from God and that charity brings justice. This influences Jews to help the poor, for example by volunteering at a food bank or supporting Jewish charities that help refugees.
points: Tzedakah as a mitzvah (duty): influences regular giving, maaser, tzedakah boxes
Wealth as a loan from God: influences generous sharing
Charity brings justice (tzedek): influences work for fairer society
Leviticus 19 (leaving gleanings) / Proverbs 25:21: even enemies should be helped
Examples: volunteering, food banks, Jewish charities, sponsorship
Each way: 1 mark for the belief and 1 mark for how it influences Jews

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the sanctity of life influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe life is sacred because humans are made in God's image. This influences many Jews to carry organ donor cards, because organ donation can save a life and saving life is a very important mitzvah.

Another way is that Jews follow Pikuach Nefesh, the duty to save a life. This influences Jews such as doctors to work on Shabbat in an emergency, even though work is normally forbidden.
points: Life sacred, made in God's image (Genesis 1:27): respect for every person
Pikuach Nefesh: doctors and others break Shabbat laws to save life
Organ donation and medical research supported by many Jews
Sanhedrin 4:5: saving one life is like saving a world; influences helping in emergencies
Opposition to euthanasia and caution on abortion
Each way: 1 mark for the belief and 1 mark for how it influences Jews

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about life after death. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that the dead will be physically resurrected when God decides. Many Orthodox Jews believe this, which is why they bury the dead and do not cremate. Maimonides' 13th principle of faith says God will bring the dead back to life, and Ezekiel 37:12 says 'I will open your graves and bring you up from your graves'. This means Orthodox Jews are influenced to bury their dead with care so the body is ready for resurrection.

Another belief is that the soul is immortal and God judges it. Many Reform Jews hold this view and do not insist on a physical resurrection. Daniel 12:2 says that many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame. This means Jews are influenced to live a good life now, because they believe God will judge them on how they treated others and kept the mitzvot.
points: Belief 1: bodily resurrection (Orthodox), supported by Ezekiel 37:12, Isaiah 26:19, Maimonides' 13th principle
Belief 2: immortality of the soul and judgement (Reform and many others), Daniel 12:2
Other creditable beliefs: Olam Ha-Ba, Gan Eden, Gehinnom, Sheol, gilgul
Source of wisdom: Tenakh, Talmud, Pirkei Avot, Maimonides
Application: burial practice, living ethically, focusing on this life
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each belief

exam.q: Explain two ways in which the Covenant with Abraham is important for Jews today. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that the covenant gives Jews their identity as God's chosen people. God promised Abraham that he would be the father of a great nation, saying in Genesis 12:2 'I will make you into a great nation and I will bless you'. This means Jews see themselves as having a special responsibility to serve God and to be a light to others.

Another way is that the covenant created the practice of Brit Milah. In Genesis 17:10-11 God tells Abraham that every male must be circumcised as the sign of the covenant. This means Jewish families today circumcise their baby sons on the eighth day to keep the covenant and show that the child belongs to the Jewish people.
points: Chosen people/special relationship and responsibility (Genesis 12:1-3; Deuteronomy 7:6)
Brit Milah as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:10-11)
Promised Land: connection to Israel, aliyah, Jerusalem (Genesis 17:8)
Abraham as a role model of faith and obedience (Genesis 22)
Numerous descendants (Genesis 15:5): continuity of the Jewish people
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each way

exam.q: Explain two ways in which the Ten Commandments are important for Jews today. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that the Ten Commandments are a central part of the covenant at Sinai. They are in Exodus 20:1-17 and begin 'I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt'. This means Jews see them as direct commands from God and read them in synagogue and display them above the ark.

Another way is that they guide how Jews live and treat others. The fourth commandment says to remember Shabbat and keep it holy, and the sixth forbids murder. This means Jews today keep Shabbat as a day of rest and treat life as sacred, because they believe obeying these commandments is part of keeping their promise to God.
points: Part of the covenant with Moses at Sinai: direct from God (Exodus 19-20)
Foundation of the 613 mitzvot
Guide for commandments between people and God (Shabbat, no idols) and between people (no murder, theft)
Displayed in synagogues and read at Shavuot
Different views: Orthodox treat all as binding, Reform as moral guidance
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each way

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about free will and the mitzvot. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that God gave humans free will so they can choose between good and evil. Deuteronomy 30:19 says 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Choose life'. This means Jews are responsible for their choices, so they try to make good choices and keep the mitzvot.

Another belief is that the mitzvot are binding for Orthodox Jews but a guide for Reform Jews. Orthodox Jews believe God commanded all 613 mitzvot, so they keep them strictly, while Reform Jews use informed free will to choose which mitzvot give their life meaning. Pirkei Avot 3:15 says 'everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given', which supports using free will within God's law.
points: Free will: humans choose good or evil; judged on choices (Deuteronomy 30:19; Pirkei Avot 3:15; Maimonides)
613 mitzvot: 248 positive and 365 negative
Mitzvot between people and God, and between people
Orthodox: binding; Reform: informed choice
Source of wisdom: Torah, Pirkei Avot, Maimonides
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each belief

exam.q: Explain two ways in which Jews put the idea of Tikkun Olam (healing the world) into practice. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One way is by working for social justice and helping those in need. Isaiah 42:6 says Jews should be 'a light to the nations'. This means many Jews volunteer, give to charity and campaign for fairness, for example by supporting refugees, in order to make the world a better place.

Another way is by caring for the environment. Psalm 24:1 says 'The earth is the Lord's and everything in it'. This means Jews believe the world belongs to God, so many Jews take part in recycling, tree planting and conservation as a way of looking after God's creation.
points: Tikkun Olam: repairing the world through social justice, charity, peace work
Environmental care and stewardship (Psalm 24:1; Deuteronomy 20:19)
Isaiah 42:6, 'light to the nations'; Talmud 'not for you to finish the work'
Links to the Messianic Age (especially Reform)
Examples: volunteering, Tzedek and other charities, campaigning
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each way

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about God as Law-Giver and Judge. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that God is the Law-Giver who gave the Torah and 613 mitzvot to the Jewish people. Isaiah 33:22 says 'the Lord is our lawgiver', and in Deuteronomy 10:12-13 God asks Jews to keep His commandments for their own good. This means Jews study the Torah and try to follow the mitzvot because they believe this is how to live a holy life.

Another belief is that God is a fair judge who judges everyone by their actions. Genesis 18:25 asks 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?' This means Jews try to live honestly and treat others fairly, and they repent on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur because they believe God will judge them.
points: God as Law-Giver: Torah, 613 mitzvot, covenant at Sinai (Isaiah 33:22; Deuteronomy 10:12-13)
God as Judge: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and after death (Genesis 18:25; Psalm 75:7)
Loving and merciful: forgives those who repent (Exodus 34:6)
Application: following mitzvot, repentance, ethical behaviour
Marks: 1 point + 1 development + 1 source/application for each belief

exam.q: 'Belief in the Messiah is the most important Jewish belief.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The Messiah is one of Maimonides' 13 Principles of Faith, so for many Orthodox Jews it is a core belief. They pray for him daily in the Amidah.
Belief in the Messiah gives hope in persecution and suffering. Jews have been persecuted for centuries, and the promise of a Messianic Age of peace (Isaiah 2:4) has helped them endure.
It motivates action: Jews who want the Messianic Age to come keep the mitzvot or work for justice, so the belief shapes how they live.
against: The belief that God is One (the Shema) is more basic. Without it there is no Judaism, and the Messiah only matters because God is One and God will act.
Many Reform Jews do not expect a personal Messiah, so for them it cannot be the most important belief.
The covenant and the mitzvot shape daily life more than a future event. Jews keep Shabbat and kosher food laws now, whether or not the Messiah comes.
exam.conclusion: The Messiah is important, especially for Orthodox Jews, but belief in God as One and the covenant are more fundamental, because the Messiah depends on them.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that belief in the Messiah is the most important belief. Maimonides listed the coming of the Messiah as one of his 13 Principles of Faith, and Orthodox Jews pray for him three times a day in the Amidah. The belief gives hope. Jews have faced persecution for centuries, and the promise of a Messianic Age of peace, when nations 'will not take up sword against nation' (Isaiah 2:4), gives meaning to suffering. It also influences behaviour, because Jews who want to bring the Messianic Age nearer keep the mitzvot carefully or work for justice. This is a strong argument for Orthodox Jews, because the Messiah is linked to the Temple, resurrection and the final judgement, so it connects to many other beliefs.

However, there are strong arguments against. The Shema says 'the Lord is One', and belief in one God is the foundation of Judaism. Without this belief, the Messiah would have no meaning, as he is sent by God. In addition, many Reform Jews do not expect a personal Messiah at all and instead see the Messianic Age as something humans must create through Tikkun Olam. For them the belief cannot be the most important. Finally, the covenant and mitzvot affect Jewish life every day, in Shabbat, prayer and food laws, whereas the Messiah is a hope for the future.

Overall, I think belief in the Messiah is very important, particularly as a source of hope, but it is not the most important belief. The Messiah depends on belief in God as One and on the covenant, which give Jews their identity and daily practice, so these are more fundamental. This is supported by the fact that Jews of all traditions accept the Shema, while only some accept a personal Messiah.

exam.q: 'The Ten Commandments are all Jews need to live a good life.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17) cover the most important duties to God and to others: worship one God, keep Shabbat, honour parents, do not murder, steal or lie.
They were given directly by God at Sinai as the core of the covenant, so they have the highest authority.
Many Reform Jews see the ethical commandments as the heart of Judaism, giving a simple guide for modern life.
against: The Torah contains 613 mitzvot, and Orthodox Jews believe all are binding, covering food, dress, prayer and festivals that the Ten Commandments do not mention.
The Ten Commandments do not mention charity, kindness or Tikkun Olam, which Jews believe are essential (Leviticus 19:18, Micah 6:8).
Jews also rely on the Talmud and rabbis to interpret how to apply the law, so the Ten Commandments alone are not enough.
exam.conclusion: The Ten Commandments are a vital foundation, but most Jews believe a good life also needs the other mitzvot and the Oral Law, so the statement is not convincing.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that the Ten Commandments are enough to live a good life. They were given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 20:1-17) and cover the central duties: to worship only God, to keep Shabbat, to honour parents, and not to murder, steal or lie. These laws cover duties to God and duties to other people, so they form a complete moral base. Many Reform Jews believe the ethical teaching of the Torah is more important than ritual laws, so they would see the Ten Commandments as a clear, simple guide for modern life. This is a reasonable argument, because if everyone followed them, society would be fairer and safer.

However, most Jews would disagree. The Torah contains 613 mitzvot, and Orthodox Jews believe that all are binding because they were all given by God. These cover areas the Ten Commandments do not mention, such as kosher food, prayer, festivals and circumcision. Furthermore, the Ten Commandments say little about kindness or charity, yet Leviticus 19:18 commands 'love your neighbour as yourself' and Micah 6:8 says God requires people to 'do justice, love kindness and walk humbly'. Jews also depend on the Talmud to explain how to apply the law in everyday life. This is a strong argument, because the Ten Commandments are short and need interpretation.

In conclusion, I do not think the Ten Commandments are all Jews need. They are the heart of the covenant and give a strong moral foundation, but Jewish tradition teaches that the whole of the Torah, with the Talmud's guidance, is needed to live as God wants. Even Reform Jews, who select among the mitzvot, would still add the teachings on justice and kindness.

exam.q: 'Saving a life is always more important than keeping Jewish law.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Pikuach Nefesh says saving life overrides almost all mitzvot, including Shabbat, kosher laws and Yom Kippur fasting.
Life is sacred because humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 says saving one life is like saving a whole world.
Leviticus 18:5 says Jews should 'live by' the commandments, so the law exists to protect life, not to cause death.
against: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 74a) says three laws can never be broken, even to save a life: idolatry, murder and forbidden sexual relations. So saving life is not 'always' more important.
Some Jews believe obeying God matters more than life itself, as in martyrdom to avoid idolatry.
A Jew cannot kill an innocent person to save another life, because all lives are equally precious.
exam.conclusion: Saving a life overrides nearly all Jewish law, but because of the three exceptions the word 'always' makes the statement too strong.
exam.model:
There is a strong case for this statement. In Judaism life is sacred, because humans are created in God's image (Genesis 1:27). The principle of Pikuach Nefesh means that the duty to save a life overrides almost all other mitzvot. A Jewish doctor can work on Shabbat, and a sick person can eat or break the fast on Yom Kippur if their life is in danger. The Mishnah says that whoever saves one life is credited as if they saved an entire world (Sanhedrin 4:5), and Leviticus 18:5 says Jews should 'live by' the laws, which suggests the law is meant to protect life. This is a convincing argument, because it shows the purpose of the Torah is to give life and not take it away.

However, the word 'always' is a problem. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 74a) teaches that there are three laws a Jew must never break, even to save a life: murder, idolatry and forbidden sexual relations. In history, some Jews chose death rather than worship other gods, because they believed obedience to God was more important than their own survival. Also, a Jew cannot kill an innocent person to save someone else, because each life is equally sacred. This is also a strong argument, because it shows Jewish law does have limits that even Pikuach Nefesh cannot change.

In conclusion, I think the statement is mostly true but not completely. In nearly every situation, saving life comes first, and this is why Pikuach Nefesh is one of the best-known Jewish principles. But because there are three exceptions, it is not true that it is 'always' more important. The exceptions actually protect sanctity of life in a different way, as they stop one life being valued over another.

exam.q: 'Jews should keep all 613 mitzvot.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Orthodox Jews believe all 613 mitzvot were given by God at Sinai as part of the covenant, so they must be obeyed (Deuteronomy 11:26-28 says obedience brings blessing).
Keeping the mitzvot is how Jews keep their side of the covenant and show faith. Jeremiah 31:33 says God's law is written on their hearts.
Mitzvot give structure and identity and unite Jews across time. Maimonides wrote that they train a person to be good.
against: Reform Jews believe in informed free will: they choose mitzvot that have moral or spiritual meaning, since some laws, such as Temple sacrifices, are impossible or outdated today.
Many mitzvot cannot be kept by everyone, for example some apply only to priests or only in Israel.
Pikuach Nefesh shows even Orthodox Jews do not keep every law in every situation, as saving life can override the rules.
exam.conclusion: The mitzvot are central to Judaism, but because some cannot be kept today and Jews are taught to use free will, it is better to say Jews should keep them as far as they can with understanding, not all of them in every case.
exam.model:
Orthodox Jews would agree with this statement. They believe the 613 mitzvot were given by God to Moses at Sinai as part of the covenant, so each one is a command that must be followed. Deuteronomy 11:26-28 says that obeying the commandments brings a blessing, and not obeying brings a curse. The mitzvot cover every part of life, including prayer, food, Shabbat and treating others fairly, so keeping them gives Jews their identity and keeps them close to God. This is a strong argument for believers, because if God is the Law-Giver, picking and choosing could be disobedience.

However, Reform Jews disagree. They believe God gave humans free will and that Jews should use informed choice to decide which mitzvot to follow. Pirkei Avot 3:15 says 'everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given'. They argue that some mitzvot, such as Temple sacrifices, cannot be kept today and that others belong to a different time. In addition, some mitzvot apply only to priests or only in the Land of Israel, so no one can keep all 613. Even Orthodox Jews accept that Pikuach Nefesh can override mitzvot to save a life. This is a convincing argument, as it shows the statement is not realistic in practice.

In conclusion, I think the mitzvot are the heart of Jewish life and should be taken seriously, especially the ethical ones. However, the statement is too strong. Not all 613 can be kept by everyone, and Jewish teaching on free will suggests that Jews should choose to follow the mitzvot thoughtfully rather than just obey every one automatically. The best answer is that Jews should keep as many as they can with understanding.

exam.q: 'Jews should focus on this life, not on life after death.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Judaism teaches that Olam Ha-Zeh (this world) is where the mitzvot are done. The Tenakh says little about the afterlife, so Jews focus on how they live now.
Tikkun Olam gives Jews a duty to repair the world today. The Talmud says 'It is not for you to finish the work, but you are not free to ignore it'.
Because Jewish beliefs about the afterlife differ widely (resurrection, immortal soul, gilgul), no one can be certain, so it is wiser to concentrate on what is known.
against: Many Jews believe God will judge each person after death, so the afterlife gives a reason to live well (Daniel 12:2).
Orthodox Jews believe in bodily resurrection (Maimonides' 13th principle), and this affects burial practice and gives comfort when someone dies.
Belief in Gan Eden and Gehinnom motivates keeping the mitzvot, because actions have consequences beyond death. Pirkei Avot says only Torah and good deeds go with a person after death.
exam.conclusion: The main emphasis of Judaism is this life, but belief in judgement and resurrection gives that life meaning, so the two cannot really be separated.
exam.model:
There is a good argument that Jews should focus on this life. Judaism teaches that this world, Olam Ha-Zeh, is where the mitzvot are carried out and where God's will is done. The Tenakh has very little to say about the afterlife, and Jewish views differ widely, from resurrection of the body to immortality of the soul or reincarnation. Since no one can be sure, it makes sense to concentrate on what is known. Tikkun Olam gives Jews a duty to heal the world now, and Rabbi Tarfon teaches in Pirkei Avot 2:16 that it is not your duty to finish the work, but you are not free to neglect it. This is a persuasive argument, as it explains why Jewish culture has stressed charity, justice and study more than speculation about heaven.

However, the afterlife is still important to many Jews. They believe God will judge each person on how they lived, as Daniel 12:2 says some will awake to everlasting life and some to shame. This gives a strong reason to behave well. Orthodox Jews believe in bodily resurrection, as Maimonides taught in his 13 Principles of Faith, and this shapes their burial customs and comforts the bereaved. Pirkei Avot 6:9 says that only Torah and good deeds go with a person when they die, which links this life directly to what comes next. This is also a strong argument, because without belief in judgement some Jews might feel less reason to keep the mitzvot.

In conclusion, I think the statement is largely right about emphasis, because Judaism is mainly concerned with how people live now. But the two ideas are connected: belief in judgement and an eternal soul gives meaning to actions in this life. So Jews should focus on this life, while keeping the afterlife in mind as the reason it matters.

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the nature of God. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that God is One. Jews are monotheists who believe God is a single, indivisible being with no body, so they reject the idea of the Trinity and never make images of God. The Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4 says 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One'. This shows that only God may be worshipped, which is why Jews recite the Shema every morning and evening.

Another belief is that God is the Creator of everything. Most Jews believe God created the universe out of nothing (ex nihilo) and still sustains it every day. Genesis 1:1 says 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth'. This means the world has a purpose and belongs to God, so Jews thank God with blessings and have a duty to look after creation as stewards.
points: God is One: monotheism, indivisible, no body, rejection of the Trinity and of idols
Source: Deuteronomy 6:4 (the Shema) or Exodus 20:3 or Isaiah 44:6 'there is no god but me'
God is Creator: ex nihilo, sustains the world, creation is good (Genesis 1:31)
Source: Genesis 1:1 or Psalm 24:1; applied to stewardship, Shabbat or blessings
Also creditable: God as Law-Giver and Judge, loving and merciful (Exodus 34:6), eternal, omnipotent, omniscient
Marks: 2 per developed belief, 1 for naming a relevant source, 1 for applying it to the belief

exam.q: 'Believing that God is One is the most important Jewish belief about God.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is the central declaration of Jewish faith, said twice daily and traditionally as a person's last words, so belief in one God is at the very heart of Judaism.
The first two of the Ten Commandments forbid other gods and idols (Exodus 20:2-4). Every other belief depends on there being one God: one Creator, one Law-Giver, one Judge.
Belief in one God is shared by Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews alike, while other beliefs (such as a personal Messiah or bodily resurrection) are disputed.
against: Belief in God as Creator could be seen as more important: the Torah begins with creation, and it is the basis of Shabbat, stewardship and the sanctity of life.
God as Law-Giver may matter most in daily life, because the 613 mitzvot shape food, prayer, Shabbat and how Jews treat others. Many Orthodox Jews see obedience to the Law as the way to please God.
God as loving and merciful Judge gives hope: Exodus 34:6 and the Days of Awe show that Jews can repent (teshuvah) and be forgiven, which affects how they live and face death.
exam.conclusion: Belief that God is One is the most important because every other quality depends on it, but the other qualities show how that one God relates to people, so they cannot be separated.
exam.model:
Many Jews would agree with this statement. The Shema, 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One' (Deuteronomy 6:4), is the central statement of Jewish faith. Jews say it every morning and evening, place it in the mezuzah on their doorposts and traditionally say it as their last words before death. The first commandments at Sinai also forbid other gods and idols. This is a strong argument, because the other beliefs about God depend on this one: if there were many gods, there could not be one Creator, one Law-Giver and one Judge. It is also the belief that unites Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews, who disagree about other things such as the Messiah.

On the other hand, some Jews might argue that God as Creator is more important. The Torah begins with 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth' (Genesis 1:1), and this belief is the basis of Shabbat, stewardship and the sanctity of human life, since humans are made in God's image. Others, especially many Orthodox Jews, might say God as Law-Giver matters most in practice, because the 613 mitzvot guide every part of daily life, from food to prayer. A Jew who has done wrong might feel that God as loving and merciful Judge is most important, because Exodus 34:6 describes God as 'compassionate and gracious', and on Yom Kippur Jews rely on God's forgiveness. These arguments are persuasive, because they show which belief affects a person most in their own situation.

In conclusion, I agree that belief in God as One is the most important. The other qualities, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge, are all ways of describing how the one God relates to the world, so they depend on it. However, Jews would not see these beliefs as competing, because together they give a full picture of the one God they worship. The statement is true as long as it is not used to make the other beliefs seem unimportant.

exam.q: 'God's mercy is more important to Jews than God's justice.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Exodus 34:6 describes God first as 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in kindness'. Without mercy no one could stand before God, since everyone does wrong.
Ezekiel 18:23 teaches God does not want the wicked to die but to turn back and live, so the aim of judgement is change, not punishment.
The Days of Awe and Yom Kippur are built on the hope of forgiveness: teshuvah, prayer and charity can change God's decree.
against: God is the 'Judge of all the earth' who must do justice (Genesis 18:25). If there were mercy without justice, the mitzvot would mean nothing and victims would be ignored.
Justice protects the weak: Deuteronomy 16:20 'Justice, justice shall you pursue'. Jews are called to copy God's justice in society.
Forgiveness for wronging others requires putting things right with the person first, so justice comes before mercy.
exam.conclusion: Most Jews would say the two cannot be separated: God's justice makes the mitzvot meaningful, and God's mercy makes repentance possible.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that God's mercy is more important. When God revealed himself to Moses, God was described as 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in kindness' (Exodus 34:6). Since every human makes mistakes, nobody would survive God's judgement without mercy. Ezekiel 18:23 teaches that God does not want the wicked to die, but to turn from their ways and live. The whole season of the Days of Awe, from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, is based on the hope that teshuvah, prayer and tzedakah can change God's decree. This is a convincing argument, because it shows that the purpose of God's judgement is to help people change, not to punish them.

However, others would argue that justice is just as important, or more so. Abraham asks 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?' (Genesis 18:25), showing that Jews expect God to be fair. If God simply forgave everything, the 613 mitzvot would lose their meaning and people who hurt others would face no consequences. The Torah commands 'Justice, justice shall you pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20), and Jews are expected to copy God's justice by standing up for the poor and powerless. Even on Yom Kippur, God does not forgive sins against other people until the wrongdoer has apologised and put things right. This is a strong argument, because it shows mercy in Judaism always comes with responsibility.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement, because Jewish teaching joins the two together. The prayer Avinu Malkeinu calls God both 'Father' and 'King', showing love and authority at the same time. Justice gives the mitzvot their seriousness, and mercy gives people hope that they can return to God. A God with only one of these qualities would not be the God described in the Tenakh.

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the divine presence (Shekhinah). Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that God's presence was made known to the Israelites in visible ways during their history. When they left Egypt, God went ahead of them as a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, and later God's glory filled the Tabernacle. Exodus 40:34 says 'the glory of the Lord filled the Tabernacle'. This shows Jews that God chose to dwell among His people, so the Shekhinah is a sign of God's closeness and care.

Another belief is that the Shekhinah is present today when Jews pray or study together. The rabbis taught that God's presence is with a minyan of ten. Pirkei Avot 3:6 teaches that when ten sit together and study Torah, the Shekhinah is among them. This means many Jews make an effort to pray with a minyan and to study Torah in groups, because they believe God is especially close at those times.
points: God's presence shown in the Tenakh: burning bush (Exodus 3), pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21), Sinai, Tabernacle (Exodus 40:34), Temple (1 Kings 8:10-11)
Present with a minyan in prayer (Berakhot 6a) and in Torah study (Pirkei Avot 3:6)
Went into exile with the Jews, never abandons them; linked to the Western Wall
Feminine, comforting presence that shares suffering
Ner tamid symbolises God's constant presence
Marks: 2 per developed belief, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: 'Jews can only experience the Shekhinah in the synagogue.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The rabbis teach that the Shekhinah is with a minyan of ten at prayer (Berakhot 6a), and the minyan usually meets in the synagogue, so the synagogue is the main place to experience it.
The synagogue is a 'small sanctuary' that replaces the Temple, where God's glory dwelt (1 Kings 8:10-11). The ark and ner tamid remind Jews of God's presence there.
Communal services such as reading the Torah need a minyan, so some of the most important moments of worship happen only in the synagogue.
against: Pirkei Avot 3:6 says the Shekhinah is present even with one person who studies Torah, so it can be felt at home or anywhere.
In the Tenakh God's presence appeared in the desert, at a burning bush and on Sinai, long before synagogues existed. Psalm 139 says there is nowhere a person can go where God is not present.

The rabbis taught that the Shekhinah went into exile with the Jews, and many feel it at the Western Wall, at the Shabbat table, in nature or in acts of kindness. Reform Jews especially stress experiencing God in everyday life.
exam.conclusion: The synagogue is a special place to experience the Shekhinah, especially with a minyan, but Jewish teaching clearly says God's presence can be felt elsewhere, so 'only' makes the statement false.
exam.model:
Some Jews might agree that the synagogue is where the Shekhinah is experienced. The Talmud (Berakhot 6a) teaches that when ten people pray together, the divine presence is with them, and a minyan normally gathers in the synagogue. Since the Temple was destroyed, the synagogue has been called a 'small sanctuary', taking the place of the Temple, where God's glory filled the building (1 Kings 8:10-11). The ark holding the Torah scrolls and the ner tamid burning above it remind worshippers that God is present. This is a reasonable argument, because public prayers like the Torah reading need a minyan, so some ways of meeting God together can only happen there.

However, there are stronger arguments against the word 'only'. Pirkei Avot 3:6 says that the Shekhinah is present when ten study Torah, but goes on to say it is present even with one person, so a Jew studying alone at home can experience God's presence. In the Tenakh, God's presence was felt at the burning bush, in the pillar of cloud and fire and on Mount Sinai, long before there were synagogues. Psalm 139 says there is nowhere a person can flee from God's presence. The rabbis also taught that the Shekhinah went into exile with the Jewish people, so it is with them wherever they live. Many Jews feel it at the Western Wall, at the Shabbat table with family, or when helping others, and Reform Jews in particular stress meeting God in everyday life.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. The synagogue is an important place to experience the Shekhinah, especially when a minyan prays together, but Jewish teaching shows that God's presence is not limited to one building. The word 'only' goes against both the Tenakh and the rabbis.

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in resurrection influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that many Orthodox Jews believe God will raise the dead bodily at the end of time. This influences them to bury the dead quickly and whole, and to refuse cremation, because the body should be treated with respect and kept ready for resurrection.

Another way is that belief in resurrection is linked to judgement, as Daniel 12:2 says some will awake to everlasting life and some to shame. This influences Jews to keep the mitzvot and do good deeds now, because they believe God will judge how they lived when the dead are raised.
points: Burial rather than cremation; body buried whole and quickly; Jewish burial societies (chevra kadisha)
Encourages keeping mitzvot and good deeds because judgement follows resurrection (Daniel 12:2)
Comfort for the bereaved: hope of reunion; mentioned daily in the Amidah ('who revives the dead')
Reform view: many reject bodily resurrection, so some accept cremation and focus on this life
Each way: 1 mark for the belief, 2 marks if the influence is clearly explained

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the role of the Messiah. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that the Messiah will bring a time of world peace. Many Jews believe the Messiah will end war and injustice so that all nations recognise the one God. Isaiah 2:4 says 'they will beat their swords into ploughshares' and 'nation will not take up sword against nation'. This shows that the Messianic Age will be a time when weapons are no longer needed, which gives Jews hope during suffering.

Another belief is that the Messiah will restore Israel. Orthodox Jews believe he will be a king from the family of David who will gather Jews from all over the world to the land of Israel and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. Ezekiel 36:24 says God will gather the people from the nations and bring them back to their own land. This means Orthodox Jews pray for the Messiah in the Amidah and keep the mitzvot, believing this prepares the world for his coming.
points: Bring world peace and justice (Isaiah 2:4, Micah 4:3, Isaiah 11:6)
A king from David's line who rules justly (Jeremiah 23:5, Isaiah 11:1-5)
Gather the exiles to Israel (Ezekiel 36:24) and rebuild the Temple
Teach Torah and lead all to recognise God (Zechariah 14:9)
Different view: many Reform Jews expect a Messianic Age not a person (Pittsburgh Platform 1885)
Marks: 2 per developed belief, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the Covenant with Abraham influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe God commanded Abraham to circumcise every male as the sign of the covenant. This influences Jewish parents to hold a Brit Milah for their baby boys on the eighth day, so that each new generation enters the covenant.

Another way is that God promised Abraham the land of Canaan. This influences many Jews to feel a deep connection to the land of Israel, for example by praying facing Jerusalem, visiting Israel, or making aliyah to live there.
points: Circumcision as the sign (Genesis 17): Brit Milah on the eighth day
Promise of land: connection to Israel, prayer towards Jerusalem, aliyah, 'Next year in Jerusalem'
Chosen people: responsibility to keep mitzvot and be a light to the nations
Abraham's faith and trust as a model: obeying God in hard times
Great nation: sense of identity and belonging, Avraham Avinu
Each way: 1 mark for the belief, 2 if the influence is explained

exam.q: 'The Covenant with Abraham is more important for Jews today than the Covenant at Sinai.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: The covenant with Abraham came first and created the Jewish people: without the promise of a great nation (Genesis 12:2) there would have been no Israelites at Sinai.
It is marked on the body of every Jewish boy through Brit Milah (Genesis 17:10-11), a practice kept even by many Jews who keep few other mitzvot.
It contains the promise of the land (Genesis 17:8), which is central to Jewish identity and prayer, and the idea of being a blessing to all families of the earth.
against: The covenant at Sinai gave the Torah and 613 mitzvot, which shape every part of daily Jewish life: Shabbat, food, prayer and ethics.
The Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1-17) apply to every Jew, male and female, while the sign of Abraham's covenant applies directly only to males.
At Sinai the whole people agreed 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exodus 24:7), making it a covenant with the nation, not one family; Shabbat, its sign, is kept every week.
exam.conclusion: Sinai probably affects daily life more, but it builds on Abraham's covenant, so the covenants are best seen as stages of one relationship rather than rivals.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that the covenant with Abraham is more important. It came first and created the Jewish people: in Genesis 12:2 God promised 'I will make you into a great nation', and without this there would have been no Israelites to receive the Torah at Sinai. It is the covenant that is marked physically through Brit Milah, as God commanded in Genesis 17:10-11, and many Jews who keep few other mitzvot still have their sons circumcised. It also includes the promise of the land, which has shaped Jewish prayer and identity for thousands of years. This is a strong argument because Abraham's covenant is the foundation of everything that follows.

However, others would argue that the covenant at Sinai matters more today. At Sinai God gave Moses the Torah, including the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:1-17 and the 613 mitzvot. These guide every part of daily life: Shabbat, kosher food, prayer and how to treat others. The whole people agreed, 'All that the Lord has spoken we will do' (Exodus 24:7), so it was a covenant with the nation, not just one family. Its sign, Shabbat, is kept every week by men and women alike, whereas circumcision directly applies only to males. Jews celebrate the giving of the Torah at Shavuot and study it daily. This is a convincing argument because it shows how the Sinai covenant is lived out constantly.

In conclusion, I think the covenant at Sinai has a greater effect on how Jews live day to day, because the mitzvot come from it. However, I would not say Abraham's covenant is less important, because Sinai fulfils the promises God made to Abraham. Most Jews would see them as two stages of the same relationship with God, so comparing them is less useful than seeing how they fit together.

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief in the Covenant at Sinai influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that Jews believe God gave the Ten Commandments at Sinai, including the command to remember Shabbat and keep it holy. This influences Jews to stop work from Friday sunset to Saturday night, light candles and attend synagogue, because keeping Shabbat is the sign of the Sinai covenant.

Another way is that Jews believe the Torah was given to the whole people at Sinai. This influences Jews to study Torah and to celebrate Shavuot, when they read the Ten Commandments in synagogue, and it is why young Jews take on the mitzvot at their Bar or Bat Mitzvah.
points: Ten Commandments: keeping Shabbat, honouring parents, not stealing or lying
Torah given at Sinai: daily study, synagogue readings, Shavuot
Chosen people: responsibility to keep the mitzvot and set an example
Each generation takes on the covenant: Bar and Bat Mitzvah
Orthodox: all mitzvot binding; Reform: ethical commandments central
Each way: 1 mark for the belief, 2 if the influence is explained

exam.q: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the role of Moses. Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One belief is that Moses was the leader chosen by God to free the Israelites from slavery. God called him at the burning bush, and he confronted Pharaoh, announced the plagues and led the people out of Egypt through the sea. This shows that God keeps His promises to Abraham's descendants, and Jews remember Moses' leadership every year at Pesach.

Another belief is that Moses was the greatest prophet, who received the Torah from God at Mount Sinai. Deuteronomy 34:10 says that no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face. This means Jews treat the Torah he received as having the highest authority, and they call him Moshe Rabbenu, 'Moses our teacher'.
points: Leader of the Exodus: burning bush (Exodus 3), plagues, crossing the sea
Received the Torah and Ten Commandments at Sinai (Exodus 19 to 20, Pirkei Avot 1:1)
Greatest prophet, spoke with God face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10; Maimonides' 7th principle)
Lawgiver and teacher (Moshe Rabbenu); some believe he wrote the Torah (Deuteronomy 31:9)
Intercessor after the golden calf; led the people 40 years in the wilderness
Marks: 2 per developed belief, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: 'Healing the world (Tikkun Olam) is the most important moral principle for Jews.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Tikkun Olam is the widest principle: it includes justice, charity and kindness, as well as care for the environment, so it sums up the others.
Rabbi Tarfon teaches 'it is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to neglect it' (Pirkei Avot 2:16): every Jew has a lifelong part to play.
Many Jews believe healing the world brings the Messianic Age closer, and Reform Judaism sees social action as the heart of Jewish life.
against: Justice may be more basic: 'Justice, justice shall you pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20) is a direct command, and without justice the world cannot be healed.
Tzedakah is a binding mitzvah with clear rules (maaser, Maimonides' ladder) and Rabbi Jonathan Sacks argued it could change the world; it is the practical way Tikkun Olam happens.
The Talmud says acts of kindness are greater than charity (Sukkah 49b); and for many Orthodox Jews keeping all the mitzvot, including ritual ones, is the true way to repair the world.
exam.conclusion: Tikkun Olam is a good summary of Jewish moral life, but it depends on justice, charity and kindness, so many Jews would see the principles as working together rather than one being most important.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that healing the world is the most important moral principle. Tikkun Olam is the broadest of the principles because it includes working for justice, giving charity, showing kindness and caring for the environment. Rabbi Tarfon taught that 'it is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to neglect it' (Pirkei Avot 2:16), which shows every Jew has a lifelong duty to make the world better. The Aleinu prayer, said at the end of every service, hopes 'to repair the world' under God's rule, and many Jews believe this work helps bring the Messianic Age closer. Reform Jews in particular see social action, such as volunteering on Mitzvah Day or supporting refugees, as the heart of their faith. This is a strong argument, because Tikkun Olam gives a purpose to all the other principles.

On the other hand, others would say a different principle is more important. Justice could be more basic, because the Torah commands 'Justice, justice shall you pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20), and a world cannot be healed while it remains unfair. Tzedakah is a clear mitzvah, not a choice: many Jews give a tenth of their income, and Maimonides set out a ladder of giving that ends with helping people become self-sufficient. The Talmud also teaches that acts of loving-kindness are greater than charity (Sukkah 49b), because they can be done for anyone, rich or poor, living or dead. Some Orthodox Jews would add that keeping all the mitzvot, including Shabbat and prayer, is the real way to repair the world, not only social action. These arguments are convincing because they are based on direct commands in the Torah and Talmud.

In conclusion, I think the statement is partly true. Tikkun Olam is a helpful way of summing up Jewish moral life, but it only happens through justice, charity and kindness. Rather than one being most important, the principles depend on each other, so a Jew who tried to heal the world without justice or kindness would not be following Jewish teaching.

exam.q: Explain two Jewish teachings about Pikuach Nefesh (saving a life). Refer to sacred writings or another source of Jewish belief and teaching in your answer. (6 marks)
exam.model:
One teaching is that saving a life overrides almost every other mitzvah. A Jew may break Shabbat, eat non-kosher food or break the Yom Kippur fast if a life is at risk, and even if it is only uncertain whether a life is in danger. Leviticus 18:5 says Jews should keep God's laws and live by them, and the Talmud (Yoma 85b) explains this means 'and not die by them'. This shows that the purpose of the mitzvot is to give life, so a Jewish doctor or paramedic will work on Shabbat in an emergency.

Another teaching is that there are limits to Pikuach Nefesh. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 74a) teaches that a Jew must never commit murder, idolatry or forbidden sexual relations, even to save their own life. This is because every human life is equally sacred, made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), so one innocent person can never be killed to save another.
points: Saving life overrides almost all mitzvot: Shabbat, kashrut, fasting (Leviticus 18:5 with Yoma 85b)
Act even when danger is uncertain (Mishnah Yoma 8:6); acting quickly is praiseworthy
Three exceptions: murder, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations (Sanhedrin 74a)
Saving one life is like saving a whole world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)
Duty to help others: 'do not stand idly by' (Leviticus 19:16); examples: Hatzolah, organ donation
Marks: 2 per developed teaching, 1 for naming a source, 1 for applying it

exam.q: Explain two ways in which belief that the mitzvot are the commands of God influences Jews today. (4 marks)
exam.model:
One way is that many Jews believe keeping the mitzvot is their part of the covenant with God. This influences Orthodox Jews to keep laws such as Shabbat and kosher food in detail every day, and to ask a rabbi how to apply halakhah when they are unsure.

Another way is that some Jews believe certain mitzvot were given for a particular time. This influences many Reform Jews to make informed choices, keeping ethical mitzvot such as charity and honesty fully, while observing some ritual laws, such as parts of the food laws, less strictly.
points: Covenant duty: obey mitzvot such as the Ten Commandments, Shabbat, kashrut
Gives identity and unity: shared patterns of dress, worship and food
Study of Torah and Talmud to know how to keep them; asking a rabbi
Reform/Liberal: informed choice; ethical mitzvot central, some ritual mitzvot kept less strictly
Sanctifies daily life: blessings, mezuzah, tzedakah
Each way: 1 mark for the belief, 2 if the influence is explained

exam.q: 'Mitzvot between man and man are more important than mitzvot between man and God.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to Jewish teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion. (12 marks)
for: Hillel summed up the whole Torah as 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour' (Shabbat 31a), putting treatment of others at the centre.
Mishnah Yoma 8:9: Yom Kippur atones for sins against God but not for sins against people until they are appeased, suggesting harming people is harder to put right.
The prophets criticised worship without justice (Amos 5:21-24) and Micah 6:8 asks for justice and kindness; many Reform Jews stress ethical mitzvot.
against: The first commandments are about God, and the Shema commands love of God 'with all your heart' (Deuteronomy 6:5). Love of neighbour flows from love of God.
All mitzvot come from the same God, so Jews should not rank them. Pirkei Avot 2:1 warns to be as careful with a light mitzvah as a weighty one.
Mitzvot between man and God (Shabbat, prayer, food laws) build the identity and discipline that make ethical living possible, and many Orthodox Jews see them as equally binding.
exam.conclusion: Both kinds come from God and support each other, so most Jews would reject ranking them, though treating others well is a clear test of whether worship is sincere.
exam.model:
Some Jews would agree that mitzvot between man and man are more important. When asked to teach the whole Torah standing on one foot, Hillel replied, 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; the rest is commentary' (Talmud, Shabbat 31a). The Mishnah (Yoma 8:9) teaches that Yom Kippur brings forgiveness for sins against God, but not for sins against another person until that person is appeased. This suggests that hurting people is harder to put right. The prophets also criticised people who worshipped God but ignored justice, and Micah 6:8 says God requires people 'to do justice and love kindness'. Many Reform Jews therefore see ethical mitzvot as the heart of Judaism. This is a strong argument, because worship that ignores other people seems empty.

However, other Jews would disagree. The Ten Commandments begin with duties to God, and the Shema commands Jews to love God 'with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might' (Deuteronomy 6:5). For many Orthodox Jews, all 613 mitzvot come from the same God at Sinai, so it is wrong to rank them. Pirkei Avot 2:1 teaches that a person should be as careful with a minor mitzvah as with a major one, because they do not know the reward of each. Mitzvot such as Shabbat, prayer and food laws shape Jewish identity and remind Jews of God throughout the day, which helps them treat others well. Even Hillel's saying ends 'go and learn', pointing back to the whole Torah. This is a convincing argument, because love of neighbour in Judaism is based on belief in God who created every person in His image.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. Mitzvot between people are a vital test of sincere faith, but they cannot be separated from mitzvot between people and God, because both come from the same covenant. Most Jews see them as two sides of one way of life.
